limitations: No limitations section - the paper has no section acknowledging its own limitations

The only concession to confounding is a single sentence conceding the higher proportion of synchronous tumours in the biopsied group, immediately dismissed on the grounds that synchronicity did not affect survival within the non-biopsied group
The authors note that neither of two comparable prior series was able to demonstrate an effect of biopsy on long-term survival
critique: The exposure is not randomised and is not even a decision made at this centre - every biopsy happened at a referring hospital before referral. Group 1 is therefore defined by having been managed elsewhere by clinicians who thought biopsy was needed, which is a proxy for diagnostic uncertainty, more advanced or atypical disease, and a different referral pathway. The paper tests biopsy and measures referral route

The one large baseline imbalance is in the variable most strongly linked to prognosis: 61% of biopsied patients had synchronous disease versus 26% of non-biopsied, p<0.001. The authors dismiss this by showing synchronicity did not predict survival within group 2 only - a subgroup in which synchronous patients are, by construction, those who did not get biopsied, i.e. the ones whose diagnosis was obvious. That is not a valid adjustment, and no multivariable model including synchronicity is shown

The claimed independent effect of biopsy is attributed to 'Cox's proportional hazard model' in the methods but reported in the results as 'P = 0.001, Student's t test'. No hazard ratio, no confidence interval and no covariate list appear anywhere. The central inferential claim of the paper is unverifiable from the paper

The denominator for the survival comparison is 598 patients who all underwent curative-intent resection and all had histologically confirmed metastases. Conditioning on resection removes everyone whose biopsy-track deposit or disseminated disease made them inoperable - the very harm the paper attributes to biopsy. If biopsy causes dissemination, the patients most harmed never reach the denominator, and the direction this bias pushes the survival estimate is not discussed

A 14.2% absolute difference with a 95% CI of 2.0-26.4% is reported alongside a declaration that the study provides 'overwhelming support' for the hypothesis. An interval whose lower bound is 2% does not support that language, and the paper's title states causation ('causes tumour dissemination and adversely affects survival') from an unadjusted observational comparison

Needle-track deposits were 'specifically sought at the time of surgery' in a centre whose surgeons held a strong prior against biopsy, and the deposit definition required localisation to the biopsy site - a judgement made by the same unblinded surgeons. Ascertainment of the exposure's signature harm was neither blinded nor independently adjudicated

Nineteen percent is far higher than the 1-3% needle-track rates reported for percutaneous biopsy generally, and sits alongside an unexplained equivalence between open and percutaneous biopsy (22% vs 15%). That open biopsy at colorectal resection produces as many 'needle-track' deposits as a percutaneous needle suggests the lesions being counted include peritoneal implantation from the laparotomy itself, which is a different mechanism from needle tracking

Eighteen years of accrual (1986-2003) with imaging that changed from CT and CT arteriography to routine MRI during the study, and with the biopsied patients concentrated in the earlier era by the nature of referral practice. Era is an uncontrolled confounder for both staging accuracy and chemotherapy availability, and no analysis by period is presented

The 1.2% inadvertent benign resection rate - the counterweight that makes forgoing biopsy acceptable - is computed as 6/514 using a denominator of non-biopsied patients plus a quantity that does not match the 508 reported in the main comparison, and rests on six events. All six were benign cysts or haemangiomas in a unit with intraoperative ultrasound and a specialist hepatobiliary surgeon; it cannot be transported to a general surgical setting

Survival is reported as 4-year overall survival only, with no disease-free survival despite a section heading promising it, no recurrence pattern, and no cause-specific analysis. If biopsy causes peritoneal dissemination, the mechanism predicts a specific recurrence pattern that the data could have tested and did not

Perioperative outcomes are reported with means and s.e.m. for skewed variables (length of stay 11(8) vs 11(3) days) and significance tested by Student's t test; chi-squared is used for cells containing single events (1 vs 8 perioperative deaths)
Single centre, single surgical team, retrospective analysis of a prospective database, no sample size calculation, no correction for multiple comparisons across 10 baseline and 5 outcome comparisons
15997444.n: 598 patients resected with curative intent for colorectal metastases (from 925 liver resections); 90 biopsied before referral, 508 not biopsied
15997444.bottom_line: In 598 patients resected for colorectal liver metastases at one specialist centre, those biopsied before referral had needle-track deposits in 19% and a 14% lower 4-year survival - it establishes that preoperative biopsy of resectable colorectal metastases is associated with worse outcome and that inadvertent resection of benign disease is rare (1.2%) in expert hands, and it cannot establish causation, since the biopsied group was referred from elsewhere, had 61% versus 26% synchronous disease, and the adjusted analysis is reported only as a p-value from the wrong statistical test.
15997444.funding: Not stated; acknowledgement of a named data collector only

limitations: Lack of pathological proof in the majority; benignity was defined by imaging or CT stability, with biopsy of all small lesions achieved in only three patients
In patients with multiple lesions, progression of one lesion classified the patient as malignant, leaving the nature of the remaining lesions unproven

Patients with cancer and 6-12 month stability may harbour stable or slow-growing metastases; six of 29 such patients (21%) had interval chemotherapy or immunotherapy that may have produced apparent stability and overestimated benignity

Technical variation between serial scans (contrast dose, volume, rate, agent) could not be guaranteed, making comparison less sensitive; significant technical variation affected 8 of 99 patients classified as stable
Volume averaging, slice-location differences and respiratory excursion could cause lesions to be missed
No attempt was made to characterise lesions by margin or density because partial-volume effects dominate at this size
critique: The denominator is 1454 *contrast-enhanced abdominal CT examinations in outpatients at a tertiary referral centre*, 82% of whom had a known cancer or prior hepatic metastases. This is not a general population and not an incidental-finding population - these scans were ordered to look for metastases. The 17% figure is a case-mix artefact and should never be quoted alongside Karhunen's autopsy 52% or Kaltenbach's ultrasound 15% as if the three measured the same thing

The '17%' and the '51% benign' share a denominator problem in opposite directions: 17% is per-examination among cancer-surveillance outpatients, while 51% is per-patient among those with lesions, with 27% simply unclassified and dropped from neither numerator nor denominator cleanly

The reassuring claim that no patient without known malignancy had a malignant lesion is built on 45 patients of whom 23 had inadequate or no follow-up and none had biopsy. The paper itself calls the group 'small'; the effective denominator is 22, which cannot exclude a malignancy rate of 10% or more

15 mm is a threshold chosen to match the technology of 1989-90: 10-mm contiguous non-helical sections on a single scanner. Both the detection threshold and the lesion spectrum differ from modern thin-section multidetector CT, so the 17% cannot be transported forward, and the authors do not attempt to say in which direction it would move

Verification is differential and informative: lesions that grew were verified by growth, lesions that did not grow were verified by not growing, and lesions never followed were called indeterminate. There is no independent reference standard anywhere in the study, so benign and malignant are defined by the index test's own behaviour

Interval cytotoxic therapy in part of the stability group means some 'benign' lesions were treated metastases - the authors flag this for 6 patients but do not report treatment exposure across the whole >=12-month group
Retrospective single-centre single-scanner design, no second reader, no measure of interobserver agreement for detecting sub-15 mm lesions, which is precisely where reader variability is greatest

Chi-squared tests across number-of-lesion strata with no adjustment for the correlation between lesion number and tumour burden, so the 'number of lesions predicts malignancy' gradient is confounded by stage
1738990.n: 1454 consecutive outpatient CT examinations; 254 patients (17%) with lesions <=15 mm, of whom 209 had known cancer and 45 did not
1738990.bottom_line: Among outpatients undergoing contrast CT at a cancer-heavy tertiary centre in 1989-90, 17% had a hepatic lesion 15 mm or smaller and roughly half of those were probably benign even with known cancer - it establishes that small lesions are common and often benign in a cancer-surveillance population, and establishes nothing about prevalence or probability in an unselected or truly incidental population.

limitations: Comparative long-term survival data between patients with and without seeding were unavailable and would have benefited the meta-analysis
Needle biopsy techniques varied between included studies, as did the completeness with which all seedings were detected, although all diagnosed seedings were histologically confirmed

Fine-needle aspiration is highly operator-dependent and requires close clinico-pathological correlation; false negatives from inadequate sampling and from mistaking HCC for regenerative or dysplastic nodules occurred in the included series

In some included studies biopsy appears to have been performed despite the diagnosis being obvious from imaging and alpha-fetoprotein, so the diagnostic role of biopsy over imaging plus AFP cannot be ascertained from these retrospective studies
The claim that a coaxial technique prevents seeding, although plausible, could only be proven by a well-designed prospective randomised controlled trial
critique: The units are wrong throughout and the error is in the abstract. The pooled estimate is reported as '0.027 (95% CI 0.018 to 0.040)' described as 'a patient with seeding per 100 patients', then converted in the conclusions to '2.7% overall'. If 0.027 were per 100 patients the rate would be 0.027%; the figure is in fact a proportion, 2.7%. The same confusion recurs for the per-year figure ('0.009 per 100 patients per year' = 0.9% per year). A pathway reading the abstract literally would misstate the risk by a factor of 100

Seven of eight studies are retrospective, and the only prospective study reported zero events in 239 patients - the single largest and methodologically strongest contribution pulls the estimate down, while the highest rate (5.8%) comes from the smallest series (59 patients) in which one seeded lesion was over 10 cm with grossly elevated AFP (so biopsy was unnecessary) and another also received intralesional alcohol, an acknowledged confounder. The pooled 2.7% is an average over studies that were asking different questions of different patients

Ascertainment of the outcome is a direct function of follow-up duration, which varied from a median of 14 months to 44 months across studies, against a median time-to-seeding of 17 months and a reported range out to 4 years. Maturen's zero-event study used a 30-day minimum follow-up threshold and a mean of 410 days; a study that stops looking before the median event time cannot contribute a meaningful zero. Pooling these as if they measured the same quantity guarantees underestimation, and the paper's homogeneity test (p=0.684) is reassuring only because low-power studies with few events cannot be distinguished from each other

Zero events were handled by two approaches - excluding the study or substituting 0.5 - and the paper reports only that this 'did not make a difference to the overall estimates'. With 2 of 8 studies at zero and 26 events in total, continuity-correction choice is not a minor sensitivity analysis and the alternative results are never shown

The denominator is patients with histologically proven HCC who were biopsied. It excludes by construction anyone whose biopsy was non-diagnostic and who was therefore never confirmed, and anyone whose seeding was discovered after they had been removed from a transplant list and lost to hepatobiliary follow-up. The striking claim that 'no patient who developed seeding subsequently underwent liver transplantation' is reported as reassurance when it is equally consistent with seeding having disqualified those patients from transplant - the paper does not distinguish the two readings

The claim that seeding never affected survival rests on narrative citation of individual series with no survival analysis, no comparator and, as the authors concede, no comparative survival data at all. With 26 events spread across eight series there is no power to detect a survival effect, so 'did not impact survival' means 'was not shown to impact survival'

The paper's own framing - 2.7% seeding risk against 10-20% one-year post-transplant mortality - compares a complication rate with a mortality rate from a different procedure in a different population, as though they were commensurable. Needle-track seeding does not substitute for transplant mortality; the correct comparator would be the harm from a false-positive or false-negative imaging diagnosis, which the paper quantifies for neither

The diagnostic-performance figures that would justify biopsy at all come from a single included study and are misreported in the discussion as 'nodules with diameters of 2 mm or less' where the methods and the source say 2 cm. The adjacent sentence cites a median time to seeding of '17 months.5-48', a corrupted reference marker printed inside a numerical result

Quality assessment was narrative: the first three authors reviewed the eight papers and assessed design, outcome measures, potential biases and case mix, but no instrument (QUADAS, Newcastle-Ottawa) was applied, no per-study risk-of-bias judgement is reported and no sensitivity analysis by quality was performed

No funnel plot, no Egger test, no assessment of publication bias of any kind in a literature where a seeding event is publishable and a negative series is not, and where the authors explicitly did not search for unpublished material

Needle gauge, number of passes and amount of normal parenchyma traversed are named in the introduction as determinants of seeding risk, and then not analysed - no subgroup or meta-regression by any of them, despite Huang's series containing an internal comparison (Vim Silverman 4/126 = 3.2% vs Tru-cut 5/329 = 1.5%) that the review quotes without pooling

Search was limited to PubMed, EMBASE and NCBI to March 2007, supplemented by 'general Internet searches' and the authors' personal paper collections - a non-reproducible component of the search strategy
Single-centre authorship from a liver transplant unit with an institutional interest in the biopsy question; competing interests declared as none
18669577.n: 8 studies, 1340 patients with HCC, 26 seeding events; median follow-up 17 months
18669577.bottom_line: Pooling 1340 biopsied patients with proven HCC across eight observational studies, needle-track seeding occurred in 2.7% (95% CI 1.8-4.0%) or 0.9% per patient-year and never demonstrably affected survival - it establishes an order of magnitude for the risk, around 1 in 37 patients, and it does not establish a reliable figure, since seven of eight studies were retrospective, the largest prospective study found zero events, follow-up was shorter than the median time to seeding in several series, and the abstract misstates the units by a factor of 100.
18669577.funding: Not stated; competing interests declared as none. Acknowledgement to a librarian for search assistance

limitations: The paper states its recommendations are intended to be flexible, in contrast to standards of care, and are based on relevant published information plus the experience of the authors
It concedes studies of post-biopsy complications are generally underpowered because of the rarity of serious events
It states the optimal length of post-biopsy observation has not been firmly established
It notes transvenous mortality may reflect selection of higher-risk patients
It acknowledges controversy on ultrasound guidance, on fine-needle aspiration of small HCC, and on repositioning after biopsy, and notes wide practice variation in the HCC biopsy question
It notes precise mortality figures vary widely in the literature
critique: The harms quoted throughout are drawn from series of biopsy for *diffuse parenchymal disease*, not for a focal mass, and the paper says in one clause that death from bleeding 'may be greater after biopsy of malignant lesions'. The 1 in 2500 to 1 in 10,000 severe bleeding figure and the 1 in 10,000 mortality figure are explicitly for the intercostal percutaneous approach in diffuse non-focal disease. A pathway that applies them to biopsy of a vascular hepatic mass is importing the wrong denominator, and the paper never supplies the right one

The quantified risks are ranges and single-citation point estimates with no confidence intervals anywhere: severe bleeding as a fourfold range, mortality as 'the most commonly quoted figure', seeding as 0.13% from one study. No pooled estimate, no meta-analysis, no systematic search is described

The seeding figure of 0.13% sits an order of magnitude below the 2.7% that Silva's meta-analysis of HCC biopsy reports in the same depot. Both are in the literature; this guideline cites the low one and defers the HCC biopsy question to a separate document, so a reader using the AASLD paper alone gets a seeding risk twenty times lower than the pooled HCC-specific figure

A large share of recommendations are Class I Level C - the committee's strongest recommendation grade supported by its weakest evidence grade. Dedicated physical space, vital-sign monitoring every 15 minutes, management of anticoagulants and several others are all Class I Level C, which means 'you should do this' resting on expert opinion

The observation-time recommendation (2-4 hours, Class I Level B) contradicts the evidence cited to support it: a 3214-patient series reduced recovery from 6 hours to 1 hour with no change in complication rate, a 500-patient series discharged 496 at 1 hour, and the text itself concludes 'prolonged observation times appear to be unnecessary'. The recommendation is then set at 2-4 hours without explanation of the gap between the data and the number

The hydatid guidance reverses a long-standing absolute contraindication on the basis of 'available data suggest' with no number of cases, no anaphylaxis rate and no comparison to the WHO-IWGE consensus (also in this depot) which treats cyst puncture as requiring resuscitation equipment, a surgical back-up team and mandatory albendazole prophylaxis. A pathway taking the AASLD sentence alone would aspirate a hydatid cyst without any of those precautions

The image-guidance evidence is internally contradictory and left unresolved: one 631-patient comparison found no advantage for real-time ultrasound over prebiopsy marking, while a large unblinded randomised trial found a fourfold reduction in major complications (0.5% vs 2.2%). The paper reports both and issues no recommendation strong enough to settle practice, which is honest but leaves the pathway without guidance on the step most likely to affect harm

Published 2009, drawing on a literature that predates routine thin-section multidetector CT and modern coaxial and plugged-track techniques, and predates the current era of molecular subtyping that changes why one would biopsy a mass at all. No update interval or expiry is stated

The one randomised trial underpinning the ultrasound recommendation was unblinded, and the paper reports the result without discussing how unblinding affects a pain endpoint measured at 36.4% versus 47.3%

No systematic search strategy, no databases, no dates, no inclusion criteria for the literature review, and no formal evidence tables - so the 'formal review and analysis of the recently published world literature' cannot be reproduced or audited
Conflicts of interest for the five authors are not reported in the available text

The focal-lesion indication table marks 'other focal lesions' as an indication for biopsy with no stratification by lesion type, size, risk category or whether resection is contemplated - the distinctions on which Jones 2005 and Silva 2008 turn
19243014.bottom_line: The AASLD position paper on liver biopsy, establishing that severe bleeding occurs in roughly 1 in 2500 to 1 in 10,000 and death in about 1 in 10,000 percutaneous biopsies, that tumour seeding is around 0.13%, and that 2-4 hours of observation suffices - the harm figures derive from biopsy for diffuse parenchymal disease rather than for focal masses, most of its procedural recommendations are Class I Level C expert opinion, and it concedes its own complication literature is underpowered.
19243014.funding: Not stated; an AASLD position paper approved by the association

limitations: The watch-and-wait approach for inactive cysts is stated to 'deserve formal evaluation' - the authors flag it as unvalidated while recommending it
Long-term evaluation of non-PAIR percutaneous techniques is stated to be unavailable, so caution is advised before drawing reliable conclusions
For extrahepatic sites the authors state the strength of recommendation is even lower than for hepatic CE because of lower disease frequency
Calcification is stated to be unreliable as an indicator of non-viability: more frequent in CE4 and CE5 but observable at all stages
The consensus closes by stating it will help promote studies that provide the missing evidence to be included in the next update - an acknowledgement that the evidence base is currently absent
critique: Essentially the entire document is Strength of recommendation B, Quality of Evidence III - the IDSA category for expert opinion and descriptive studies. Of the eleven graded recommendations in the text, ten are B/III and one is C/II. There is not a single A-grade or Level I recommendation in a consensus that governs whether a cystic liver lesion is punctured, operated on or ignored

The search was Medline only, English only, 1980-2008, supplemented by the authors' personal files. Cystic echinococcosis is concentrated in regions whose literature is substantially Turkish, Chinese, Spanish, Arabic and Russian; restricting to English in a WHO document on a disease of the Mediterranean, Central Asia and South America systematically excludes the primary evidence. No search string, no yield count, no screening process and no eligibility criteria are reported, and final consensus was reached by email with no voting, no Delphi rounds and no agreement thresholds

The safety claim for PAIR rests on 'data from more than 4000 PAIRs over a period of more than 20 years' with no citation, no denominator for any specific complication, and no anaphylaxis rate. Anaphylaxis is the catastrophic outcome that makes this document matter for an incidental cystic lesion, and the consensus never states its frequency - it only requires that resuscitation equipment be available

The assertion that complications are 'no more frequent after PAIR than after surgery' is sourced to a single 1999 comparison. A non-randomised comparison between a minimally invasive and an open procedure, with selection by cyst stage, cannot support an equivalence claim, and none is quantified

Albendazole prophylaxis is called 'mandatory' on the authority of the 2003 WHO-IWGE document and a 1988 paper - i.e. the strongest word in the document attaches to a recommendation with no trial evidence and no stated effect size

The watch-and-wait recommendation for CE4/CE5 is supported by one cited long-term ultrasound follow-up study and the honest admission that the approach 'deserves formal evaluation'. A pathway that adopts watch-and-wait for an inactive-appearing cyst is adopting a strategy the consensus itself describes as unevaluated

Stage assignment - the hinge on which every management decision turns - is a subjective ultrasound judgement, and no interobserver agreement is reported anywhere for the CE1-CE5 classification. The document simultaneously notes that calcification, the most objective feature, is unreliable for viability and can occur at any stage, and that MR spectroscopy and other adjuncts are unsettled

The CL (unclassified) category is where a genuinely incidental cyst of unknown nature sits, and the document's only guidance is that CL cysts should not be treated until the parasitic nature is proven - without specifying how to prove it in a seronegative patient, given that serology requires two tests of opposite performance characteristics whose sensitivities and specificities are nowhere stated

No sensitivity or specificity is given for any diagnostic test in the document: not ultrasound staging, not the high-sensitivity or high-specificity serological assays it requires in sequence, not CT, not MRI. A pathway cannot compute a post-test probability from this consensus

The size thresholds (5 cm for PAIR plus benzimidazole versus benzimidazole alone; 10 cm for continuous catheter drainage; 10 mL daily output to stop drainage) are single numbers with no derivation and single supporting citations
The alveolar echinococcosis 2 cm radical-resection margin is stated as a definition of radicality with no supporting outcome data and no comparison to narrower margins

Published 2010 and described as the first major revision in over a decade; no expiry date, no update interval and no living-guideline mechanism, so a 2026 pathway may be relying on a search that stopped in 2008
No conflict-of-interest declarations for the writing panel appear in the available text, and the panel is self-selected by WHO nomination with no reported external review
19931502.bottom_line: The WHO-IWGE expert consensus establishing stage-specific management of hepatic echinococcosis - PAIR plus albendazole for active CE1 and CE3a cysts over 5 cm, benzimidazole alone for small ones, surgery or other percutaneous techniques for CE2 and CE3b, and watch-and-wait for inactive CE4 and CE5 - and it establishes none of this on better than expert opinion, with ten of eleven graded recommendations at Strength B / Quality of Evidence III, an English-only Medline search closing in 2008, no anaphylaxis rate for cyst puncture, no interobserver data for the staging on which everything depends, and a watch-and-wait strategy the authors say still awaits formal evaluation.
19931502.funding: Not stated; developed under the aegis of the WHO Informal Working Group on Echinococcosis, meeting hosted in Urumqi and chaired by the WHO-IWGE coordinator and a WHO representative

limitations: Both patients suspected of having and patients known to have metastases were pooled even though the two populations have inherently different diagnostic thresholds; a known metastasis lowers the threshold for calling a second lesion positive, and inadequate reporting made subgroup analysis impossible. The same applies to synchronous vs metachronous lesions

A composite reference standard (intraoperative palpation, intraoperative ultrasound, histopathology, follow-up) was unavoidable; restricting to intraoperative plus histopathology alone would have left only one eligible study, and even then selection bias would prevent extrapolation to the general colorectal cancer population
Because an independent reference standard is used in most patients, such studies are always level 4 evidence by Centre for Evidence-based Medicine criteria
No study performed complete staging (lung, extrahepatic and liver together), even among the PET/CT studies
FDG PET and PET/CT data were scarce because most recent studies measured change in clinical management rather than diagnostic performance
Publication bias could not be excluded; authors were not contacted for unpublished per-patient or per-lesion data because authors are often unwilling to provide it

Considerable heterogeneity in sensitivity and specificity across studies, driven by study design, patient characteristics, technical aspects and data reporting; random-effects models were used but heterogeneity remains a concern that influences certainty of conclusions
Reference test details were too poorly described to permit subgroup analysis of different reference standards
Observers were not blinded to authors, affiliation or journal during data extraction
Follow-up scheme was clearly described in only one of the 39 studies
critique: The paper reports two different sets of per-patient sensitivities and never reconciles them: the abstract and Table 4 give CT 83.6%, MRI 88.2%, FDG PET 94.1%, while the 'Advances in Knowledge' box gives 81.2%, 93.4% and 94.2%. The p=.025 CT-vs-PET comparison is quoted from the first set and the MRI superiority impression from the second
Table 5 labels the small-lesion subgroup as '<1 mm' where the text and the rest of the paper mean <10 mm. A pathway reading the table alone would import a nonsensical threshold

This is a meta-analysis of *patients with histologically proven colorectal cancer being staged for liver metastases*. The denominator is a cancer-staging population with a high pre-test probability. Its sensitivities cannot be transported to an incidentally detected lesion in a normal liver, where prevalence is low and positive predictive value collapses - the paper reports no predictive values at all, only sensitivity and specificity

Per-patient sensitivity is the figure that gets quoted (94.1% for PET) and is the one the authors themselves say 'probably leads to overestimation'; the per-lesion figures that matter for deciding whether a resection is complete are 74-81%, meaning one lesion in four to five is missed by every modality

The confidence intervals on the headline per-patient numbers are enormous and are usually dropped when cited: CT 66.9-92.8% and MRI 64.8-96.8%. A 95% interval spanning 65% to 97% does not support ranking modalities, yet the paper's 'Implications for Patient Care' box declares MRI the preferred first-line modality

The modality comparison is largely between studies rather than within patients. Only the <10 mm and >=10 mm subgroups used head-to-head comparison studies (5 CT and 8 MRI data sets). Everywhere else CT and MRI estimates come from different populations with different prevalences, and the authors note interstudy variability explains the CT-MRI differences they do find

Multiple data sets were extracted from single studies (61 MRI data sets from 18 studies, 38 CT data sets from 25 studies) - readers and techniques were each counted as separate data sets. The adjustment was to add 'the same number for each study' in the random-effects subject statement, which is not a standard clustering correction and is never validated or compared with alternatives

Verification is differential and incorporation bias is structural: in 23 of 39 studies follow-up imaging was part of the reference standard, so a lesion seen on the index CT or MRI and still seen later is confirmed by the index test's own modality. The authors state investigators are 'never blinded to earlier test results' because patient care takes priority - i.e. review bias is built into every included study by design

'Prospective' here means the index test was planned before the reference test, not that patients were consecutively enrolled with a pre-specified protocol. Table 2 shows the basis of patient selection was 'Unknown' in 19 of 39 studies, and QUADAS found the largest variation in exactly this domain. The restriction to prospective studies therefore buys less internal validity than the title implies

Restricting to treatment-naive patients, while methodologically clean, selects for patients proceeding toward resection, who are by definition those whose disease looked resectable on the index imaging - a selection on the index test result

Three negative findings that should restrain equipment and protocol claims are reported and then not carried into the conclusions: multidetector CT was no better than single-section, dual-phase no better than portal-phase alone, and liver-specific contrast agents gave no benefit. The paper instead concludes MRI is preferred, resting on a date-of-publication subgroup (post-2004) that is confounded with every other secular change in practice
No GRADE or equivalent certainty rating, and no sensitivity analysis excluding the studies at highest risk of bias
20829538.n: 39 articles, 3391 patients (1863 male, 1317 female); mean age 61.4 years, range 20-93
20829538.bottom_line: Pooling 39 prospective studies of 3391 treatment-naive colorectal cancer patients, MRI, CT and FDG PET detect 74-81% of liver metastases per lesion with MRI better than CT only below 10 mm - it establishes that no modality finds every metastasis in a staging population and that liver-specific contrast and multidetector CT add nothing measurable, and it establishes nothing about how any modality performs on a low-prevalence incidental lesion.

limitations: The committee states its consensus processes meet ACR policy standards but do not meet any specific formal national standards, and that its product should be termed guidance and recommendations rather than guidelines

Information about the cost-effectiveness of pursuing incidental findings is stated to be largely lacking, so achieving a consensus of experts supported by available literature is offered as a reasonable interim objective

For the renal recommendations the committee states plainly that 'no data are yet available to support this approach'; for adrenal masses on low-dose unenhanced CT it states it is not aware of any helpful literature and the recommendations represent consensus based on members' clinical experience
The committee acknowledges the risk that its own guidance could increase rather than reduce utilisation, and explicitly identifies academic-radiologist bias toward imaging overuse as a reason
Four organ systems were addressed and others deliberately deferred

The algorithms are stated to address the most commonly encountered scenarios with exceptions depending on individual presentation, and to be inapplicable in limited life expectancy or severe comorbidity
critique: Every numerical threshold in the liver algorithm - 0.5 cm, 1.5 cm, 20 HU, 6-month follow-up, 4 cm for FNH-versus-adenoma, age 40 for the low/average risk split - is a consensus number with no derivation, no validation cohort, no sensitivity or specificity, and no citation to a study that tested it. The paper is candid that cost-effectiveness data are lacking, but it does not say that diagnostic-accuracy data for its own cut-points are equally absent

The 52% background prevalence figure is attributed to a textbook chapter rather than to Karhunen's primary autopsy series, and is presented without its denominator (95 Finnish men aged 35-69 at targeted autopsy). Stripping the source of its population is what converts a pathology observation into a clinical prior, and this white paper is the step at which that happens

The 36% figure for liver metastases in patients dying with cancer comes from the same single textbook citation and is placed in the same sentence as the 52%, inviting the reader to treat two incommensurable autopsy statistics as a risk comparison

The three risk tiers were abandoned seven years later in Gore 2017, which merged low and average risk into one category, and the size strata changed from 0.5/1.5 cm to 1/1.5 cm and the follow-up interval from 6 months to 3-6 months. No new evidence is cited in the 2017 revision for any of these changes, which means the 2010 numbers were not evidence-based and neither are their replacements. A pathway citing either document is citing a committee's preference at a point in time

Age 40 as the boundary between low and average risk is stated without any supporting data, and the 2017 revision retains 40 only as a within-category qualifier - so the same number performs two different structural roles in the two documents

The biopsy harm figures (morbidity 2.0-4.8%, mortality 0.05%) are an order of magnitude higher for morbidity than the AASLD position paper in this same depot, and are quoted as a range across three references without stating which population or technique produced them

The committee's own admission of academic overuse bias is the most important sentence in the paper and is never operationalised: no external review by generalists, health economists, primary-care physicians or patients is described, no attempt to calibrate recommendations against measured downstream utilisation, and no plan to audit whether the guidance increased imaging. Having identified the bias, the committee proceeded to write detailed follow-up algorithms anyway

Participants were recruited from ACR members who were also fellows or members of three radiology societies - a single-discipline panel. Unlike the 2017 liver revision, there is no hepatologist and no surgeon on the liver subcommittee as described in the consensus-process section

The consensus method is informal and unquantified: iterative circulation and revision with no voting, no Delphi rounds, no agreement thresholds and no record of dissent, except for the reporting-language question where the committee states it could not reach consensus and reports the disagreement openly

No systematic literature review, no evidence tables, no grading of evidence or strength of recommendation anywhere in the document - the contrast with the GRADE-based EASL guidelines in this depot is total

The liver flowchart's own footnotes are internally inconsistent with the text: the text defines the three risk tiers with oral contraceptive use under high-risk hepatic risk factors, while footnote 3 adds anabolic steroid use, and footnote 5's benign-features definition permits 'sharp, but irregular margins' while footnote 7's suspicious-features definition lists 'ill-defined margins' - leaving irregular-but-sharp margins to the reader's judgement with no guidance on the distinction
Disclosures are not reported for the full committee in the available text; the 2017 successor paper shows several liver-subcommittee members with industry relationships

The 20 HU threshold is given as 'up to about 20 HU' and elsewhere 'more than about 20 HU' - a cut-point qualified by 'about' in a document whose purpose is to standardise, with pseudoenhancement acknowledged as a reason a benign cyst may exceed it and radiologists' discretion invoked to resolve it
20889105.bottom_line: The founding ACR white paper on abdominal incidental findings, setting out a three-tier liver risk stratification with 0.5 cm, 1.5 cm, 20 HU and 6-month thresholds - it establishes a shared vocabulary and a reproducible decision structure, and it establishes none of its numbers empirically: the committee states its process meets no formal national standard, that cost-effectiveness data are largely lacking, and that academic radiologists may be biased toward imaging overuse such that its own guidance could increase utilisation.
20889105.funding: Not stated. Dr Pickhardt, Dr Berland and Dr Pandharipande disclose industry relationships in the successor 2017 paper; no disclosure block is present in the available text of this document

limitations: Microbiological data are deficient; the interaction between Klebsiella pneumoniae or Streptococcus bovis bacteraemia and specific cancers, especially colorectal, could not be investigated

Pyogenic liver abscess may be insidious with non-specific presentation, so the diagnosis may be difficult and underestimated, and some hepatobiliary cancers may have been misdiagnosed initially as abscess
Artificial registry bias when establishing the dataset cannot be entirely excluded by screening with ICD-9-CM codes, and incomplete discharge coding may limit investigation of some comorbidities

The authors acknowledge that the differential early and late risk supports two distinct hypotheses - abscess as the initial manifestation of occult cancer, versus long-term carcinogenesis following abscess - without being able to separate them
critique: The entire headline effect is detection, not causation, and the paper half-concedes this without following through. An SIR of 360 for all cancers and 1153 for biliary cancer within the first 90 days to one year cannot be a biological effect of an abscess; it is the result of imaging and endoscoping a patient intensively. The authors note that some hepatobiliary cancers 'may be misdiagnosed initially as PLA' - which is the mechanism, not a footnote. A pathway reading this as 'liver abscess causes cancer' inverts the direction: in a substantial share of cases the cancer caused the abscess, or the abscess was the cancer

The 90-day minimum follow-up requirement does not solve the reverse-causation problem and may worsen it: it removes patients who died quickly (often from the undiagnosed cancer) while retaining the surviving patients who go on to be diagnosed, so the surviving cohort is enriched for diagnosable cancer

The expected counts for the rarest outcomes are absurdly small, and the SIRs built on them are unstable. Biliary cancer within one year has an expected count of 0.02 cases, giving an SIR of 1153 with a 95% interval of 694-1801; in women the expected count is 0.01, giving 2086.73 (1077-3645). Reporting a standardised incidence ratio to two decimal places on an expected count of 0.01 is numerically meaningless, and several cells have zero observed events (biliary cancer in viral hepatitis, SIR reported as '0')

The denominator for every SIR is the 2007 Taiwanese general population adjusted for age and sex only. Liver abscess patients are 47.6% diabetic, 7.8% cirrhotic, 11.0% with chronic kidney disease and heavily skewed to men; none of these is adjusted for in the main comparison. The stratified analyses show cirrhosis alone moving the liver-cancer SIR from 4.21 to 59.77, which demonstrates that the unstratified 7.87 is a confounded average

Using the 2007 single-year population rate as the expected rate for a cohort accrued and followed 1996-2008 ignores the secular rise in Taiwanese cancer incidence and in diagnostic intensity over that period, biasing SIRs upward for the earlier accrual years

Exposure is defined purely by ICD-9-CM 572.0 appearing more than twice in claims, with no imaging, no culture, no aspirate and no clinical validation. The authors cite validation studies for diabetes and stroke coding in this database but offer none for liver abscess - the one code the whole study rests on. Nor is it clear whether the two-code requirement selects for larger, more complex or more thoroughly investigated abscesses

The outcome is also claims-defined, via a catastrophic illness certification that requires cytological or histological evidence - which is a strength for specificity but means cancer ascertainment depends on a patient applying for a co-payment exemption, a process that favours patients already in specialist care

There is no internal comparator. A matched cohort from the same 1,000,000-person sample - matched on diabetes, cirrhosis, hepatitis and healthcare utilisation - was available in the dataset and was not constructed. Comparing to external national rates instead maximises the apparent effect and prevents any adjustment

The clinically actionable conclusion ('further surveys should be conducted for the detection of occult cancers') is offered with no yield estimate, no proposed modality, no stratification by the risk factors the paper identifies, and no account of the harms or cost of surveying 1257 patients to find the excess cancers

The persistent elevation beyond 5 years - SIR 1.52 (1.09-2.05) - is the only estimate consistent with a genuine late effect, and its lower bound is 1.09. This, the most defensible finding in the paper, is given one sentence, while the detection-driven 360-fold figure is in the abstract

Subgroup SIRs are reported across cancer type, sex, two age bands, five follow-up windows, cirrhosis status, viral hepatitis status and diabetes status - well over a hundred estimates - with no correction for multiplicity and no pre-specification
Median follow-up is reported as 3.33 years with a standard deviation of 3.45, an incoherent pairing (medians do not have standard deviations) repeated in the abstract and Table 1
The paper's relevance to an incidental liver mass runs the other way from how it is usually cited: it is evidence that a lesion called an abscess may be a cancer, not that an abscess will become one
22779737.n: 1257 patients with pyogenic liver abscess and no prior cancer; 186 incident cancers over a median follow-up of 3.33 years (s.d. 3.45)
22779737.bottom_line: In 1257 Taiwanese patients with claims-coded pyogenic liver abscess, standardised cancer incidence was 3.8-fold higher overall, 7.9-fold for liver, 34.6-fold for biliary tract and 5.3-fold for colorectal cancer, with risk concentrated in the first 90 days to a year - it establishes that a liver abscess warrants a search for occult hepatobiliary and colorectal malignancy, and it does not establish that abscess causes cancer, since the near-term SIRs of 250-1150 are detection artefacts and the cohort was compared with the general population without adjustment for its 48% diabetes and 8% cirrhosis prevalence.
22779737.funding: Declaration of personal and funding interests: None

limitations: The guideline states that advances in knowledge of vascular liver disorders are hampered by the small number of cases and a limited number of studies assessing natural history, pathophysiology or therapy
It states explicitly that where no clear evidence existed, recommendations were based on the agreed opinions of the writing committee members
It states it will not cover all possible vascular disorders of the liver and is based mainly on one 2012 conference's agenda
It concedes that characterisation of BCS nodules cannot rely on the HCC criteria validated in cirrhosis, and that the only formal recommendation is multidisciplinary surveillance
It states the role of factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene variants in BCS and PVT remains unresolved, and that no single diagnostic test exists for INCPH
critique: For an incidental liver mass pathway, the load-bearing figure is that 60-80% of Budd-Chiari patients have multiple hypervascular nodules under 4 cm in a non-cirrhotic liver - the exact appearance that triggers a confident diagnosis of FNH or multifocal FNH-like lesions. The guideline reports this as a prevalence within BCS and never addresses the inverse question a radiologist faces: given multiple hypervascular nodules in a non-cirrhotic liver, what is the probability of underlying vascular disease? That conditional is absent, and the 60-80% range is given with no denominator, no source cohort and no citation in the sentence itself

The 4% cumulative HCC incidence at a median 5 years in BCS is a single cited figure with no confidence interval, no denominator and no competing-risk treatment in a population whose mortality from portal hypertension is substantial. Cumulative incidence without accounting for the competing risk of death from liver failure overstates or understates the clinically relevant risk depending on direction, and the guideline does neither

The biopsy criteria for a BCS nodule - three or fewer nodules, 3 cm or larger, heterogeneity or venous-phase washout, change on two consecutive studies, or rising AFP - come from one cited source and are offered as suggestions in the same paragraph that states the only formal recommendation is surveillance. A pathway inherits five specific triggers with no sensitivity, specificity or validation, immediately qualified by a statement that none of the established criteria apply in this setting

The A1 grade attached to 'screen patients with BCS for HCC' is the strongest grade in the document and is attached to a recommendation with no stated screening modality, no interval, no evidence of mortality benefit from screening in this population, and an underlying 4% cumulative incidence derived from one study. No screening trial in BCS exists, so the A cannot refer to the screening question

The guideline is built on the agenda of a single 2012 monothematic conference and states openly that it will not cover all vascular disorders - so the omissions are a function of what was discussed in Tallinn rather than of what a clinician encounters. Porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder, the entity that the 2026 multisociety consensus in this depot was written to define, appears here only as 'idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension' with the acknowledgement that no single diagnostic test exists

PubMed only, with no search string, no date limits, no screening process, no yield and no evidence tables. As with the companion benign-tumours guideline, GRADE labels are applied to a literature assembled by unstated means

Prevalence figures for aetiological factors are pooled from heterogeneous sources and reported as single percentages without intervals - MPN 40.9%, JAK2V617F 41.1%, thrombophilia in Western INCPH 40%, FVL in BCS with an explicitly unresolved role. These are the figures that drive a thrombophilia workup after an incidental nodule finding, and none carries an uncertainty estimate

Doppler sensitivity for BCS is given as 'more than 75%' with no specificity, no interval, no reference standard and no operator-experience stratification, while the next sentence makes the recommendation conditional on an experienced sonographer being available - so the stated performance applies only under a condition the guideline cannot assume

The statement that INCPH patients are 'often radiologically misclassified as cirrhotic' is the most practically important warning in the document for anyone reading a nodular liver, and it is given without a misclassification rate

Recommendations are presented as numbered blocks in the published text without the specific evidence grade adjacent to every clinical statement in the narrative, so a reader extracting a claim from the body text cannot always tell whether it was graded at all

No expiry date, no update interval and no living mechanism; published 2016 on a 2012 conference, meaning the evidence base is up to a decade older than a 2026 pathway citing it, in a field the guideline itself says is changing rapidly
Writing committee composition, voting procedure, agreement thresholds, external review and conflict-of-interest management are not described in the available text
26516032.bottom_line: The EASL guideline on vascular liver diseases, establishing that 60-80% of Budd-Chiari patients harbour multiple small hypervascular benign nodules in a non-cirrhotic liver, that HCC nonetheless arises in about 4% by 5 years, and that the HCC criteria validated in cirrhosis do not apply to these nodules - it is the document that should stop a pathway calling multiple hypervascular non-cirrhotic nodules FNH without excluding outflow obstruction, and it does not establish the inverse probability a radiologist actually needs, nor any validated biopsy trigger, resting as it does on a PubMed-only search built around one 2012 conference agenda with committee opinion where evidence was absent.
26516032.funding: Not stated; developed under EASL auspices following the June 2012 EASL monothematic conference in Tallinn

limitations: No limitations section - narrative review with no stated methodology

The authors explicitly concede no studies have addressed the differential diagnosis with cystic metastases, and that their own view that cystic metastases are larger with more ill-defined borders is 'based on our experience'
They note VMC with predominantly fibrous content may not be visible on MRI at all
They state it is impossible to consider genetic screening for diffuse VMC or to regularly monitor VMC patients

They acknowledge the two competing pathogenetic models conflict: the hypothesis that cysts arise from progressive dilatation of VMC contradicts the currently accepted pathophysiology of ductal plate malformations and ADPKD that they set out earlier in the same review
critique: There is no denominator anywhere behind the malignancy claim. 'About 35 cases of cholangiocarcinoma associated with VMC' is a count of case reports accumulated over roughly fifty years, set against an autopsy prevalence of 5.6% - which in a population the size of Europe implies tens of millions of carriers. The implied risk is vanishingly small, but the review's framing ('VMC... have a potential for malignant transformation') and its placement alongside the 1%/4%/7% figures for congenital hepatic fibrosis, choledochal cyst and Caroli disease invites a pathway to assign VMC a comparable risk. It is not comparable, and the review never computes or states the absolute risk

The 1%, 4% and 7% cholangiocarcinoma figures for the other ductal plate malformations are all traced to a single 1977 reference (Bloustein), and are presented without denominators, confidence intervals or any note of their age

Publication bias is the entire mechanism of the malignancy literature: a VMC found incidentally and never causing trouble is not reportable, whereas a cholangiocarcinoma found next to VMC is. The molecular evidence of 'neoplastic potential' rests on loss-of-heterozygosity analysis in two patients and a Ki-67 gradient in a four-case series - findings that establish that transformation can occur, not how often

The 5.6% autopsy prevalence is a single secondhand figure from one 1996 series; no range, no confidence interval, and no acknowledgement that autopsy detection of sub-5 mm lesions is as search-dependent as in Karhunen's series

No search strategy, no databases, no date limits, no eligibility criteria, no quality appraisal of any cited study, and no reporting standard followed - so the reader cannot tell what was left out, and the statement that MRI is 'the best imaging tool' is unsupported by any pooled accuracy estimate

No diagnostic accuracy data of any kind: not one sensitivity, specificity or predictive value for the MRI features the review recommends relying on. The claim that MR cholangiography distinguishes VMC from sub-centimetre metastases - the single most clinically consequential assertion - is supported by narrative citation only, with no study of consecutive patients and no reference standard

The signature finding, 'signal identical to CSF on heavily T2-weighted sequences', is an unquantified visual judgement with no reported interobserver agreement, and the review simultaneously concedes that fibrous-predominant VMC may be invisible on MRI - i.e. the test fails in an unknown fraction of cases and the review does not estimate that fraction

The 'enhancing mural nodule in 9/11 patients' figure comes from one study of 11 patients and is reported without interval; cited as if it were a feature rather than an 82% point estimate on 11 observations

Figure 4 in the review is itself a demonstration that the imaging logic fails in practice: two sub-centimetre lesions in a patient with colon carcinoma, one visible only on T1/T2 and one only on diffusion; intraoperative ultrasound failed to confirm the segment 2 lesion, and only serial follow-up resolved one as VMC and the other as a growing melanoma metastasis. The review draws no conclusion about how often this happens

Single-centre authorship with no multidisciplinary or pathology co-authors on a review that makes pathological and genetic claims; no systematic conflict-of-interest statement beyond a one-line declaration

The genetic transmission concern (PKHD1 in one family of three siblings) is raised as an open question - 'the possibility for an asymptomatic carrier of VMC to transmit Caroli disease or ARPKD' - with n=1 family and no population data, yet it is the kind of sentence a pathway can convert into a counselling recommendation
26522945.bottom_line: A narrative single-centre review establishing that Von Meyenburg complexes are common (about 5.6% at autopsy), that CT and ultrasound cannot distinguish them from small metastases while heavily T2-weighted MRI and MR cholangiography usually can, and that cholangiocarcinoma has arisen within them in roughly 35 reported cases - it does not establish any quantified diagnostic accuracy for those MRI features, nor any absolute malignant risk that could justify surveillance.
26522945.funding: Not stated; the authors declare no competing interest

limitations: Retrospective design, so genotypic subtyping of adenoma - which the authors note has transformed understanding of the entity - cannot be captured

The authors attribute their markedly lower FNH and adenoma prevalences to the size and age structure of the study population and to improved differentiation by modern ultrasound equipment, i.e. they concede the figures are equipment- and population-dependent

Study results across the literature are acknowledged as difficult to compare because of differences in population selection, sample size and diagnostic method (US, CT, MRI or autopsy), which is offered as the explanation for published haemangioma ranges of 0.1-20% and cyst ranges of 0.06-17.8%
No comparison was possible with other studies on the age, sex or size distribution of adenoma because no comparable ultrasound series exists
Lower focal fatty sparing than Kratzer et al is ascribed to a higher rate of prior cholecystectomy in a hospital population
critique: The denominator is 45,319 *examinations performed in a German university hospital ultrasound unit over 11 years*, mixing 55.1% inpatients and 44.9% outpatients referred for 'a variety of diseases'. A tertiary hospital ultrasound population is sicker, older and more liver-disease-enriched than the general population, so 15.1% is not a population prevalence - yet the title's 'hospital patients' is routinely dropped when the figure is quoted

The denominator is also patients, not people: anyone scanned repeatedly over 11 years could in principle be counted more than once, and the paper never states whether records were de-duplicated by patient identifier

The numerator excludes malignancy entirely. Metastases, HCC, cholangiocarcinoma, abscess and biliary hamartomas were never counted, so this study cannot speak to the pre-test probability of malignancy in an incidental lesion - which is the only question a pathway asks. Citing 15.1% to reassure a patient conflates 'prevalence of five specific benign findings' with 'probability that this lesion is benign'

Two of the five entities are not lesions at all. Focal fatty sparing (6.3%) is a pseudolesion and simple cysts (5.8%) are not tumours; together they are 80% of the 15.1%. The prevalence of a solid benign tumour is 3.6% + 0.18% + 0.04%, under 4%, which is a different clinical message

The paper contradicts itself on two headline numbers: the abstract says at least one lesion in 15.1% (n=6839) and haemangioma in 3.3% (n=1640), while the results and Table 3 say n=6851 and 3.62%. Neither the 12-patient nor the 0.3-percentage-point discrepancy is acknowledged, and 1640/45,319 = 3.62%, so the abstract's 3.3% is simply wrong

Ascertainment is asymmetric by design: FNH and adenoma required confirmation by CEUS, MRI or histology, while cysts, haemangiomas and fatty sparing were accepted on B-mode and Doppler criteria alone. Requiring a second test only for the rare entities will drive their counts down relative to the common ones, which is the most likely explanation for FNH and adenoma coming in an order of magnitude below every prior series - an explanation the authors do not consider, preferring population age and equipment quality

No confidence intervals anywhere. The adenoma estimate is 19 events, where the 95% interval is roughly 0.024-0.063%; the FNH estimate is 81 events. The paper states these to two decimal places as though precise

Operator-dependence is unquantified: 'experienced physicians' across five scanner models (Philips HDI 3000, HDI 5000, IU22, Toshiba Aplio 500, Siemens Acuson S3000) over 11 years, with no interobserver agreement, no blinding, and no reference standard for the three entities accepted on B-mode alone

Mean FNH size is reported as 51.6 mm (SD 29.5) and mean adenoma size 39.0 mm (SD 27.5) - far larger than typical incidental lesions. If only large FNH and adenomas were detected and confirmed, the prevalence estimate is of large lesions, and the conclusion that 'the finding of a FNH or an adenoma is rarely a random discovery' is partly a restatement of the detection threshold

Patients with polycystic liver disease were excluded, which lowers the cyst count, while patients with hepatic steatosis - the precondition for focal fatty sparing - were retained; the composition of the 15.1% therefore depends on two opposite selection decisions
26830608.n: 45,319 patients (21,988 women, 23,331 men), mean age 56 +/- 18.1 years (range 4 months to 105 years); 6851 (15.1%) with at least one lesion of interest
26830608.bottom_line: In 45,319 ultrasound examinations at one German university hospital, 15.1% had at least one of five pre-specified benign findings - but four fifths of that figure is focal fatty sparing and simple cysts, malignant lesions were never counted, and FNH (0.18%) and adenoma (0.04%) came in roughly tenfold below every prior series; it establishes that cysts, fatty sparing and haemangiomas dominate benign sonographic findings in a hospital population, and does not establish a general-population prevalence or any probability of malignancy.
26830608.funding: Not stated; open access publication fees covered under a Springer open-access agreement. Ethics approval 377/13, University of Ulm

limitations: The guideline's own grading is its statement of limitation: not one recommendation in the document rests on evidence level I or II-1, i.e. there is no randomised or non-randomised controlled trial evidence anywhere
Incidence and prevalence data for HCA are stated not to be well established
The 30-40 fold increase in HCA incidence with long-term oral contraceptive use is described as 'assumed'

Imaging cannot identify beta-catenin-activated HCA or distinguish it from unclassified HCA or HCC by any technique - the subtype with the highest malignant potential is radiologically invisible as a subtype
Precise counting of HCA by imaging is acknowledged as challenging, which is why the adenomatosis terminology was abandoned
No data support elective caesarean section for adenomas under 5 cm

The guideline states that if significant doubt remains, biopsy or resection may be appropriate, but these are invasive procedures associated with risk and should only be pursued after consideration by an experienced MDT
critique: The prevalence figures are presented as ranges spanning two orders of magnitude - haemangioma 0.4-20%, FNH 0.4-3% at autopsy versus 0.03% clinically - and the guideline does not resolve them or explain what drives the spread. A pathway that quotes '5% of people have a haemangioma' is selecting one point from a 50-fold range whose extremes come from autopsy and imaging series that counted different things, exactly the denominator problem that runs through this depot

The HCA prevalence of 0.001-0.004% is cited from two references and is three to four orders of magnitude below the 0.04% that Kaltenbach reports in the same depot from 45,319 ultrasound examinations. Neither figure is reconciled against the other anywhere, and both appear in current practice documents

The 5 cm resection threshold for women - the single most consequential number in the guideline - carries evidence level II-3 (multiple time series or dramatic uncontrolled experiments) and recommendation strength 2 (weak). There is no cohort in which 5 cm was derived as a cut-point, no comparison of outcomes above and below it, and no stated bleeding or malignancy risk at 4 cm versus 6 cm. The number is a convention

The rule that all HCAs in men be resected irrespective of size is also II-3 / weak, and rests on the observation that male HCA is over-represented among malignant transformations in surgical series - a denominator problem, since male HCA is rare and surgical series are enriched for resected (hence suspicious) lesions. No absolute risk is given for a small HCA in a man, so the pathway cannot compare the risk of the tumour with the risk of the hepatectomy

The guideline simultaneously requires that beta-catenin mutation trigger resection and states that beta-catenin-activated HCA cannot be identified by any imaging technique. Proving the mutation therefore requires biopsy of a lesion for which biopsy is discouraged, and the guideline does not address how the recommendation is to be operationalised - a circularity a pathway will have to resolve for itself

The MRI subtyping claim ('up to 80%') is graded II-2 / strong, the strongest recommendation grade in the document, on the basis of a point estimate at the top of an unstated range. Kim 2023 in this same depot shows the specificity of the key hepatobiliary-phase feature falling to 65% once H-HCA and I-HCA are excluded, i.e. precisely in the subtypes the guideline admits MRI cannot characterise

No search strategy, no databases, no dates, no screening, no evidence tables and no systematic review underlie any of the recommendations. The GRADE labels are applied to a literature assembled by unstated means, which gives the appearance of systematic grading without the substance of a systematic review
The panel is seven people, with no reported voting, no agreement thresholds, no Delphi process, no external review and no patient involvement. Dissent, if any, is invisible

Several recommendations rest on evidence level III (expert opinion and descriptive epidemiology) while carrying recommendation strength 1 (strong) - MDT referral for atypical FNH and for complicated haemangioma. Strong recommendations from expert opinion are a GRADE discordance the document does not justify

The '6 months of observation after lifestyle change' interval, the '1 year then annual' surveillance schedule for sub-5 cm HCA in women, the 'every 6-12 weeks' ultrasound in pregnancy, and the glycogen-storage-disease schedule of annual then biannual ultrasound are all single numbers with no derivation, no comparison of intervals and no evidence of benefit from surveillance at any frequency

The claim that risk in multiple HCA is driven by the size of the largest nodule rather than by number is graded only through its citations to retrospective surgical series, and sits uneasily with the finding, in the same paragraph, that microscopic adenomatous foci escape detection in up to 20% of resected livers

The chairman declares financial support from BMS and Gilead and advisory roles with eleven companies; the relevance to benign tumours is limited but the document carries no managed-conflict statement or recusal policy

Published 2016 with no expiry date, no update interval and no living-guideline mechanism, and predating the 2017 eight-subtype molecular classification that the HCA literature now uses - so its four-subtype framework is already superseded
27085809.bottom_line: The EASL guideline on benign liver tumours, establishing conservative management for typical haemangioma and FNH, lifestyle change for all hepatocellular adenoma, resection for any HCA in a man or with proven beta-catenin mutation, and resection in women at 5 cm or on growth - every one of its recommendations rests on evidence level II-2, II-3 or III with no randomised or controlled data anywhere, the 5 cm and male-sex rules are weak recommendations from uncontrolled series, and it requires a beta-catenin diagnosis it states no imaging technique can make.
27085809.funding: Not stated. Panel chair M. Colombo declares financial support from BMS and Gilead Science and advisory roles with Merck, Roche, Novartis, Bayer, BMS, Gilead, Tibotec, Vertex, Janssen Cilag, Achillion, Lundbeck, GSK, GenSpera, AbbVie, Alfa Wassermann and Jennerex

limitations: The committee states its consensus processes meet ACR policy standards but do NOT meet any specific formal national standards, that its product is not ACR Practice Guidelines or ACR Appropriateness Criteria policy, and that it should be termed 'guidance' and 'recommendations' rather than 'guidelines'

The algorithm content 'must be viewed as recommendations and should not be considered as standard of care', and radiologists should feel comfortable deviating from it in circumstances it does not represent
The algorithm addresses most but not all pathologies and clinical scenarios, and was explicitly not designed for hepatic infection or abscess
Recommendations draw from published evidence and expert opinion and were finalised by informal iterative consensus
Growth was deliberately not incorporated because thresholds vary by risk category and imaging features

The committee notes that overdiagnosis of benign or indolent lesions places patients at risk for dangerous and expensive follow-up care, and that benign incidental lesions are common even in patients with malignancy or cirrhosis, making management difficult in the absence of guidance
Detection and characterisation of small liver lesions is acknowledged to be challenging when aggressive dose-reduction techniques have been used
Low density is noted not to be definitive for a simple cyst in certain cancer patients, since metastases from ovarian cancer and GIST can be cystic
critique: The '30% of individuals older than 40' figure that opens the paper is supported by a block citation of nineteen references with no indication of which contributes what. Those nineteen include an ultrasound series of 45,319 German hospital patients, a cancer-surveillance CT series, CT colonography screening cohorts, lumbar spine MRI series, emergency abdominal CT reviews and a renal-colic series - populations with incompatible denominators and incompatible lesion definitions. There is no pooled estimate behind the 30%; it is a round number standing in for a literature that ranges from under 4% to 52% depending on what was counted and how hard anyone looked. This is the single most consequential unsourced figure a pathway inherits from this document

Every threshold is a consensus number with no derivation and no validation: 1 cm, 1.5 cm, 3 cm, 20 HU, 3-6 months, 1 year of stability. No sensitivity, specificity, negative predictive value or decision-analytic justification is offered for any of them, and no cohort is cited in which any threshold was tested

The thresholds changed from the 2010 white paper without new evidence and without acknowledgement of the change. The three risk tiers became two, the small-lesion stratum moved from 0.5 cm to 1 cm, the follow-up interval moved from 6 months to 3-6 months, and the FNH-versus-adenoma concern moved from 4 cm to 3 cm. Four numbers in the same algorithm shifted in seven years with no cited justification, which is direct evidence that they are conventions rather than findings - and the Liver Subcommittee was chaired by the same radiologist on both occasions

'Benign features' and 'suspicious features' are defined by lists of qualitative descriptors with no interobserver agreement data anywhere. Sharp versus ill-defined margin, homogeneous versus heterogeneous density, thick versus thin septa, and the judgement of whether pseudoenhancement is present are all reader calls on which the entire algorithm pivots, and the document reports no reproducibility for any of them

The 20 HU rule is self-undermining: a benign cyst may exceed it when pseudoenhancement is present, so 'radiologists' discretion is necessary', and the document separately notes that in lesions under 1 cm an accurate density measurement may not be attainable. The threshold is therefore unreliable precisely in the small lesions that make up most of the caseload

Biopsy morbidity is given as 'about 0.5%', an order of magnitude lower than the 2.0-4.8% in the committee's own 2010 white paper, with no explanation for the revision and the same kind of three-reference citation. A pathway reading the 2017 document gets a biopsy risk roughly eight times lower than from the 2010 one

Risk categorisation collapses enormously different hazards into one 'high risk' bucket: a patient with treated breast cancer, a patient with compensated hepatitis C cirrhosis and a bodybuilder using anabolic steroids are managed identically although their lesion differential and malignancy prevalence differ by orders of magnitude. The algorithm's output is therefore the same for populations with very different post-test probabilities

Growth was deliberately excluded from the algorithm, yet the text asserts that absence of growth over a year 'strongly favours' benignity and then concedes in the Lesion Growth Pattern section that both benign and malignant lesions can grow. The most informative single variable is left outside the structured pathway and reinserted as narrative advice

The algorithm is predicated on knowing the patient's clinical history - the document says it is critical - but offers no guidance for the common situation in which the radiologist does not have it, which is the default in emergency and screening settings that supply much of the 30% figure

No systematic review, no search strategy, no evidence tables, no grading of evidence or recommendation strength anywhere; the committee is explicit that this is informal iterative consensus and not a guideline, a disclaimer that routinely falls away when the algorithm is reproduced in local pathways

Panel is six radiologists plus one hepatologist and one hepatobiliary surgeon, with no pathologist, no primary-care physician, no health economist and no patient representative, on a document whose stated purpose includes limiting cost and overdiagnosis. The 2010 predecessor's striking admission that academic radiologists may be biased toward imaging overuse is not repeated here

Three of nine authors declare industry relationships, including a cofounder of a CT colonography company with personal fees from a contrast manufacturer, in a document recommending MRI over CT and specifying contrast-agent choice

The recommendation to eliminate the unenhanced CT phase 'whenever possible' sits uneasily with the algorithm's own dependence on noncontrast attenuation thresholds (<=20 HU on noncontrast and/or portal venous phase) for establishing benignity
No expiry date, no update interval and no mechanism for revision stated, in a document that is itself a seven-year revision of its predecessor
28927870.bottom_line: The ACR Incidental Findings Committee algorithm for incidental liver lesions on CT, establishing a two-tier risk stratification with 1 cm, 1.5 cm and 20 HU thresholds, no workup for sub-centimetre lesions in low-risk patients or for any lesion with distinctly benign features, and prompt MRI otherwise - it establishes a usable and widely adopted decision structure, and it establishes none of its numbers empirically: the opening '30% of individuals older than 40' rests on a block citation of nineteen incompatible studies, four thresholds changed from the 2010 version with no new evidence, and the committee states its own process meets no formal national standard and should not be read as standard of care.
28927870.funding: Not stated.
