Endorsed by the Society of Abdominal Radiology and the Society of Computed Body Tomography and Magnetic Resonance

limitations: No limitations section
The authors concede there is currently no specific diagnostic method for preoperative diagnosis and that the preoperative diagnostic rate remains quite low even with enhanced CT
They state that radiological films were not available for correlation in two of the six cases

They acknowledge that surgical expertise for liver resection is very limited in their setting and that the high recurrence rate in their series reflects incomplete excision from both incorrect preoperative diagnosis and lack of liver surgical expertise

They note the WHO has renamed these lesions mucinous cystic neoplasms but that the terminology and epithelial phenotype remain controversial, and that tumours without ovarian stroma in males may belong to a different entity
critique: Six cases from one hospital's pathology files over seven years. There is no denominator of any kind: not the number of liver cysts resected, not the number of hydatid cysts operated, not the number of cystic lesions imaged. The series can therefore say nothing about how often a cystic liver lesion is a cystadenoma, which is the only question a pathway asks. The recurrence 'rate' of 3/6 or 3/5 is a proportion of a convenience sample of six

Case selection is on the outcome: these are the cases a pathologist labelled cystadenoma. Cystadenomas misread as hydatid or simple cyst at pathology, or never sent for pathology because they were aspirated and deflated, are invisible to this design - which is precisely the failure mode the paper is about

The central diagnostic recommendation - that internal septations on preoperative CT are highly suggestive - is contradicted by the paper's own figure legend for case 3, which states the lesion had no internal septations and that this favoured cystadenoma. The feature is simultaneously offered as the diagnostic clue and, in one of the four cases with imaging, recorded as absent. No sensitivity, specificity or interobserver data exist for it in this paper or in the single reference cited

Recurrence ascertainment is incomplete and the two statements of it differ: the abstract says three cases recurred, the discussion says three of the five with follow-up. Two patients were lost to follow-up, one of them after a recurrence was already documented and surgery scheduled, so the true recurrence proportion is unknown and could be as high as 5/6

Follow-up is non-systematic - 'medical records, hospital discharge summaries, and by telephone inquiry' - with no defined interval, no imaging protocol and no minimum duration. Case 4's recurrence was detected at a few months and case 2's at nearly 5 years, so the detection of recurrence depends entirely on whether and when someone rescanned

The 20% malignant transformation figure after incomplete excision - the number that drives the paper's call for aggressive radical resection - is quoted from one reference with no denominator, no study design and no confidence interval, and no malignancy or even dysplasia was observed in any of the six cases here. The series provides no evidence for the risk it invokes to justify its recommendation

Margin status, the variable on which the entire recurrence argument turns, could not be assessed in at least three of six cases because specimens arrived in pieces and all arrived opened. The claim that recurrence is due to incomplete excision is therefore inferred rather than demonstrated
The two pathologists who reviewed the slides are two of the authors and are not independent of the original reports; no second-opinion review, no blinding and no interobserver agreement

The series is from a hydatid-endemic, resource-limited setting with acknowledged scarcity of hepatobiliary surgical expertise. Its recurrence rate is a function of local surgical capability as much as of tumour biology, which the authors state plainly - so the recommendation for 'an aggressive surgical approach' is being drawn from a series whose poor outcomes the authors attribute to surgical inexperience

Ethics approval was waived on the stated ground that the study 'did not involve actual patients, patients' images, or videos', which is inaccurate for a paper containing six patients' CT images and clinical narratives

The single male case lacked ovarian-type stroma, the defining feature, and had fibrinopurulent exudate - raising the possibility it was a different entity altogether. The authors discuss this classification problem and still count the case in the series of six
No treatment comparison of any kind: enucleation, segmental resection and radical resection are all discussed with citations but the six cases provide no basis to prefer one
29121977.n: 6 patients (5 women, 1 man), ages 28-60 years, mean 45 and median 43
29121977.bottom_line: Six resected intrahepatic biliary cystadenomas from one Karachi hospital over seven years, all mistaken preoperatively for simple or hydatid cysts, with recurrence in three of the five patients followed - it establishes that a mucinous cystic neoplasm can be indistinguishable from hydatid disease on clinical and radiological grounds and that incomplete excision is followed by recurrence, and it establishes no prevalence, no diagnostic accuracy for the septation sign, and no evidence for the 20% malignant transformation figure it cites to justify radical resection.

limitations: The report has an explicit 'Gaps and Future Directions' section stating that although each version has been informed by the best available evidence, there are insufficient high-quality data for many questions in HCC imaging

Future versions must account for regional variation in HCC epidemiology and biology and for financial and technical resource availability
critique: The most important sentence for an incidental-mass pathway is the scope restriction - LI-RADS applies only to patients with or at risk for HCC - and it is the sentence most often ignored. Nothing in this document, and nothing in the five LI-RADS evidence papers elsewhere in this depot, licenses applying an LR category to a lesion found incidentally in a normal liver. A pathway that assigns LR-3 or LR-5 to such a lesion is using a system outside its stated domain, and the resulting probability estimates are invalid because they were all derived under high HCC prevalence

The agreement data are reported in a way that flatters the system. The excellent kappas of 0.84-0.87 are for two individual features; the agreement for the output that actually drives management - the LI-RADS category - is fair for CEUS (0.30-0.39), fair to substantial for MRI (0.35-0.61) and only substantial for CT. A kappa of 0.30 for CEUS category assignment means two readers disagree on management for a large fraction of lesions, and this is reported in a subordinate clause while the 0.84-0.87 figure leads

Intermodality agreement of kappa 0.22-0.39 means the same lesion receives different LI-RADS categories on CT, MRI and CEUS in a substantial proportion of cases. The report notes CT tends to undercategorise and moves on. If category determines management, then management depends on which scanner the patient happened to enter - a fact the document states and never treats as a problem requiring resolution

No systematic search, no databases, no dates, no evidence tables, no grading of evidence or strength of recommendation, and no reporting standard. The agreement statistics are presented as narrative ranges drawn from references 73-85 with no pooling, no quality appraisal and no indication of which study produced which end of each range

LI-RADS version 2018 is presented as harmonised with AASLD, but the harmonisation was with an American guideline for an American transplant allocation system. The report is candid that Western criteria are deliberately more stringent than Asian criteria because of differing priorities - which means the categories encode a policy preference about the sensitivity-specificity trade-off, not a biological boundary. A pathway importing LI-RADS inherits that policy choice without being told it is one

The system has been revised in 2011, 2013, 2014, 2017 and 2018 with the next release scheduled for 2021. Five versions in seven years means the evidence base for any given version is thin by construction, and the accumulated accuracy literature always lags the current version - the point van der Pol's 2019 review and 2022 IPD meta-analysis both make when they report pooling across incompatible version definitions

The report is authored by the architects of the system it evaluates, including the chair of the LI-RADS steering committee, and the central evidential claim - that categories accurately stratify HCC probability - is supported by citation to a conference abstract by the same network (reference 2, van der Pol et al., ILCA 2018). This is self-assessment, and no independent external validation is cited

Governance is by a 250-member consortium with a writing group and 15 working groups, but no voting records, agreement thresholds, Delphi process or conflict-management policy are described, and no mechanism for external or patient input is reported

Threshold growth, enhancing capsule and the ancillary features are all named here as uncertain or controversial, and all three were subsequently shown weak or absent as independent predictors by the 2022 IPD meta-analysis in this depot - so the system retained features its own experts flagged as unvalidated

Several authors declare substantial imaging-industry relationships including a General Electric institutional grant, Siemens, GE, NGM, TaiwanJ and Madrigal grants, a Bayer consultancy and speakers bureau, and the senior author's extensive advisory, consulting, grant and speakers-bureau relationships across the contrast and scanner industry, alongside chairing the LI-RADS steering committee
30251931.bottom_line: A special report by the LI-RADS authors describing version 2018 and its harmonisation with AASLD, establishing that LI-RADS applies only to patients at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma, that agreement on individual major features is excellent (0.84-0.87) but agreement on the categories that drive management is only fair to substantial (kappa 0.22-0.79 across and between modalities), and that capsule reliability, ancillary features, LR-M criteria and treatment response all remain unvalidated - it is the document that defines the boundary a pathway must not cross, and it establishes no accuracy data of its own, being a narrative self-description by the system's architects.

limitations: All 17 included studies were retrospective; the authors state the lack of prospective studies is a limitation of the dataset and that prospectively following all LI-RADS observations with a combined pathology and composite reference standard may be the most ethically acceptable future design

The authors state explicitly that the 13% HCC probability for LR-2 should be considered provisional and at high risk of bias, from selection and/or verification bias, and that some LR-2 observations may have been benign at imaging and later transformed

Limited ability to evaluate relevant variables in meta-regression because of incomplete primary-study reporting (cirrhosis aetiology and Child-Pugh inconsistently given) or mixed methods (extracellular and hepatobiliary agents pooled); 6 of 17 studies were excluded from meta-regression for this reason, which could itself introduce bias
Only one study used CT alone, so no CT-versus-MRI comparison was possible; whether lesions were detected at antecedent ultrasound was unreported or unclear in 15 of 17 studies
Lesion size, individual major and ancillary features, and modality differences could not be assessed with study-level data; the authors recommend an individual participant data meta-analysis instead
Too few v2017 studies to compare v2014 with v2017
Exclusion of previously treated observations means results may not generalise to all liver observations
LI-RADS v2018 was published after the study was completed, changing threshold growth, eliminating LR-5us and reclassifying 10-19 mm arterial-phase hyperenhancing observations

Variability was highest in the categories with the largest HCC percentages, suggesting between-study variability exceeded within-study sampling error; forest plots showed several outliers, possibly from exclusion of benign observations in some studies or differing composite reference standards
Defining clinical management of these observations was beyond the scope of the study
critique: The denominator is observations in *patients already defined as high risk for HCC* - cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B, or current/prior HCC - imaged with full multiphase protocols at mostly academic centres. Every percentage in this paper is a positive predictive value conditioned on that prevalence. Applied to an incidentally detected lesion in a normal liver, where HCC prevalence is orders of magnitude lower, all of these figures fall sharply. The paper says nothing about non-high-risk patients, and a pathway that imports '38% of LR-3 are HCC' into a non-cirrhotic setting is making a prevalence error, not a reading error

The paper contradicts itself on variability in the discussion: the Results state LR-3 was among the most variable categories for overall malignancy (I-squared 46%) and the Discussion asserts 'variability between studies for LR-2 and LR-3 was lower than for higher LI-RADS categories'. Both statements are used to support different arguments in the same paper

LR-TIV is pooled at 92% overall malignancy when every contributing study reported 100%. The authors label this 'statistical noise' in a table footnote, which is an admission that random-effects pooling of proportions near a boundary produces estimates outside the range of the input data. The same mechanism silently affects the LR-5 (97%) and LR-M (93%) estimates and is never examined there

The LR-2 figure that drives the paper's most consequential recommendation - that current 'return to surveillance' guidance for LR-2 may need revision and biopsy considered - rests on 223 observations for HCC and 162 for overall malignancy, with a 95% interval of 8-22%, and the authors themselves call it provisional and at high risk of bias. Two paragraphs later they nonetheless recommend reconsidering management. A pathway should not inherit that recommendation

Verification bias is not merely possible but structural and bidirectional. For the lower categories, studies relying on pathology alone sampled only the lesions someone chose to biopsy, which enriches malignancy; for the higher categories, composite imaging criteria confirm HCC partly by LR-5 appearance on another modality, which is incorporation bias. The meta-regression result that high-risk-of-bias studies reported a *lower* LR-M HCC percentage is left unexplained ('it is unclear why'), which means the direction of the bias is unknown

The composite reference standard the review required (12 months stability for benignity) is less stringent than that used by 5 of the 8 studies that had one (18 months), so the pooled estimates mix benignity thresholds. The authors use this to explain away a discordant prior study (Ronot) but do not propagate it as uncertainty in their own estimates

Two of the 17 included studies are conference abstracts with unclear risk of bias across all four QUADAS-2 domains; they contributed 131 and 192 observations respectively - together about 9% of the dataset - with no peer-reviewed methods

Study designs were mixed, including case-control studies that fix the HCC-to-benign ratio by investigator choice. The paper acknowledges this could introduce bias and recommends cohort designs in future, but performs no sensitivity analysis excluding the case-control studies

Data from multiple readers or from CT and MRI within a study were averaged into a single estimate, which discards reader disagreement entirely. No interobserver agreement is reported for any category, although category assignment is the index test

Non-HCC malignancy data came from only 14 of 17 studies, so the HCC and overall-malignancy denominators differ in every row of the summary table (e.g. LR-5: 1705 vs 1423 observations) and the two columns are not directly comparable, a point made only in a table footnote
Observations treated before the index test were excluded, which removes the population in which indeterminate categories are most common in practice

The LI-RADS versions studied (v2014, v2017) were both superseded by v2018 before publication, and the authors could not compare versions. Several included criteria - threshold growth, LR-5us - no longer exist, so the mapping from these numbers to a current LI-RADS report is approximate and unquantified

The depot filename attributes this paper to 'Anon'; it is van der Pol and colleagues, and the first-author overlap with the 2022 IPD meta-analysis in the same depot means the two are not independent sources
30445016.n: 17 studies (all retrospective), 2760 patients, 3556 observations, 2482 HCCs and 217 non-HCC malignancies; 14 studies contributed overall-malignancy data
30445016.bottom_line: Pooling 3556 observations from 17 retrospective studies in high-risk patients, the percentage of HCC rises monotonically from 13% at LR-2 to 94% at LR-5, with LR-M 93% malignant but only 36% HCC - it establishes that CT/MRI LI-RADS stratifies HCC probability as intended within a high-risk population, and it does not establish any probability outside that population, nor a reliable LR-2 estimate, which the authors themselves label provisional and at high risk of bias.
30445016.funding: Not stated in the available text

limitations: No limitations section - narrative review

The authors repeatedly flag the thinness of the evidence they are summarising: studies comparing imaging modalities are described as sparse; several RCTs of adjuvant systemic chemotherapy for biliary cancer are said to have found conflicting results; adjuvant chemotherapy is described as of limited value so far

They state that the favourable transplant results in very early iCCA apply only to a small proportion of patients, and that the promising hepatic arterial infusion results have never been directly compared with systemic therapy

They call for predictive models of survival with and without resection against postoperative mortality risk, conceding that resection is technically feasible in patients for whom a small survival benefit may not justify the operative risk
critique: No search strategy, no databases, no date limits, no eligibility criteria, no quality appraisal of any cited study and no reporting standard. The reader cannot tell what was excluded, and every numerical claim is a single-source citation chosen by the authors

The 15% benign-on-final-pathology figure for resected apparent pCCA - the paper's own quantification of the harm of its no-biopsy policy - is cited to one reference, with no denominator, no interval and no indication of the era or centre. A major hepatobiliary resection in 15% of patients who turn out not to have cancer is a consequential number to rest on a single citation, and the review states it twice without revisiting it

The biopsy recommendation is asymmetric in its evidentiary standard. Seeding and tract recurrence are asserted as reasons to avoid biopsy with no rate, no denominator and no citation to a quantified series anywhere in the biopsy discussion, while the competing harm (15% unnecessary major resections) is given a number. A pathway reading this inherits an absolute prohibition supported by narrative and a quantified harm it is told to accept

Every survival figure is from uncontrolled surgical series. 'Five-year survival up to 60% after R0 resection' versus 'less than 10% after R1' is a comparison of patients in whom a clear margin was achievable against patients in whom it was not - which is a measure of tumour extent, not of the operation. The review presents it as the rationale for aggressive surgery without noting the confounding

The transplant figures for very early iCCA (5-year OS 65%) come from highly selected patients with well-differentiated tumours under 2 cm; the authors say so, and then the number enters the literature detached from that selection. Twelve patients transplanted after neoadjuvant chemotherapy with 25% recurrence within a year is reported as a potential expansion of indications

The hepatic arterial infusion comparison (median OS 31 vs 18 months) is explicitly non-randomised - 'no direct comparison has been performed' - with the comparator being patients who received systemic therapy alone, i.e. those not selected for an invasive pump procedure. The 20% 5-year survival is quoted in the same sentence as 'promising'

The review is authored entirely by hepatobiliary and transplant surgeons from high-volume European centres, with no radiologist, pathologist, oncologist or hepatologist co-author, on a paper that makes imaging recommendations (which modality, which phases, when to use PET), pathology recommendations (immunohistochemistry cannot distinguish iCCA from metastases) and medical-oncology recommendations (adjuvant therapy of limited value). The conclusion that patients 'should be treated only in experienced centres after referral prior to drainage' is a referral recommendation written by the recipients of referrals
No conflict-of-interest statement is present in the available text

The pCCA diagnostic criterion 'CA 19-9 elevated above 100 U/mL' is offered as one of four alternative confirmatory criteria with no sensitivity or specificity, in a paper that two sections later notes CA 19-9 rises with biliary obstruction and is unsynthesisable in 10% of patients - so the same marker is a diagnostic criterion and an unreliable test in one document

The statement that no imaging feature is unique to iCCA is the single most important sentence in the review for an incidental-mass pathway, and it is reported as one cited MRI study with no accuracy figures, no reader numbers and no reference standard. The practical consequence - that a peripherally enhancing mass in a non-cirrhotic liver cannot be called iCCA or metastasis or HCC on imaging alone - is left for the reader to draw

PET-CT is rejected on a 10% yield for occult metastases with 'low sensitivity and specificity', but neither figure is given, and the same 10% yield is described two pages earlier as a reason PET 'may be justified' in selected patients - the same number supports opposite recommendations in the two tumour sections

Recurrence data are reported from small studies without pooling (19% simultaneous intra- and extrahepatic recurrence from one series of unstated size, 54% versus 33% intrahepatic-only recurrence before and after 24 months from a 189-patient series), and 'small studies have reported favourable outcomes after resection of recurrence in selected patients' is reported without any number at all

The Key Points box asserts that multiple tumours and positive lymph nodes 'do not preclude 5-year survival after resection', which is true of any poor prognostic factor and is not a statement about expected benefit; it is the kind of formulation that justifies operating in patients the authors' own Future Research section says may not benefit
30843343.bottom_line: A narrative review by European hepatobiliary surgeons establishing that resection offers about 30% 5-year survival in perihilar and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, that no imaging feature is unique to iCCA, that preoperative biopsy is to be avoided for fear of seeding at the stated cost of 15% of resections proving benign, and that all imaging must precede biliary drainage - it does not establish any of these claims systematically, having no search strategy, no quality appraisal, no quantified seeding risk, and survival comparisons drawn entirely from uncontrolled surgical series.

limitations: The methods state that on topics where no significant study data were available, evidence was obtained from expert committee reports or from the consensus of experts at the consensus conferences
The guidelines state they provide general advice and that individual cases must be managed on the basis of all clinical data available

A dedicated section on errors and artefacts acknowledges that limitations of CEUS may result in lesion mischaracterisation, and that in select discordant cases correlation with other modalities or tissue sampling might be advised
Availability of contrast agents is noted to depend on territory-specific regulatory approval, limiting applicability

The 2012 edition is criticised by the authors for not giving evidence-based recommendations and not describing agent differences precisely - an implicit statement that the three prior iterations were expert opinion
critique: The grading is systematically discordant and this is the document's defining flaw. Of the recommendations visible in the text, several carry LoE 5 - the lowest level, expert opinion - while being labelled strong recommendations with near-unanimous votes: CEUS as first contrast modality in renal insufficiency (LoE 5, strong, 31-0), CEUS when both CT and MRI are contraindicated (LoE 5, strong, 32-0), CEUS when biopsy was inconclusive (LoE 5, weak), appropriate contrast dose and low mechanical index (LoE 5, strong), knowledge of artefacts (LoE 5, strong), and operator training (LoE 5, strong). A strong recommendation from expert opinion is a GRADE violation, and the document makes it repeatedly without justification

Conversely the two recommendations closest to the incidental-lesion question are graded in opposite directions for no stated reason. Characterising an indeterminate incidental lesion in a non-cirrhotic liver WITHOUT suspicion of malignancy is LoE 1 and strong; the same lesion WITH a history or clinical suspicion of malignancy is LoE 2 and only WEAK. The clinically higher-stakes scenario gets the weaker recommendation, and the guideline does not explain why the evidence is better in the lower-risk setting

The single LoE 1 recommendation in a 38-recommendation guideline is also the one a pathway is most likely to cite. LoE 1 implies systematic review or randomised evidence; no randomised trial of CEUS-first versus MRI-first for an incidental indeterminate lesion is cited, and the supporting narrative (references 29, 33, 45, 56-58, 62-78) is a block citation of roughly twenty studies with no pooled estimate, no accuracy figures and no quality appraisal. The grade is asserted, not demonstrated

Industry conflict is pervasive and directly relevant. The guideline recommends ultrasound contrast agents, and of the roughly 39 authors, more than twenty declare speaker honoraria, advisory board membership, consultancies or research grants from Bracco - the manufacturer of SonoVue/Lumason - and from the ultrasound scanner manufacturers whose equipment the recommendations require. The first author declares speaker honoraria from Bracco plus eleven other companies, advisory board membership with three scanner makers and research grants from three. The comparator in almost every recommendation is CT or MRI, products the funders do not sell. No managed-conflict policy, no recusal from voting, and no sensitivity of the recommendations to conflict status is described

Votes are recorded but the voters are the same experts who drafted the recommendations and who hold the declared relationships. Near-unanimity (30-0, 31-0, 32-0) in a self-selected panel is not independent corroboration, and no external review by non-sonographers, methodologists or patients is described

No systematic search strategy, no databases named beyond a parenthetical 'e.g. Medline', no date range, no screening counts, no PRISMA flow and no published evidence tables. The methods describe evidence tables as having been constructed, but they are not reproduced, so no grade in the document can be audited

The comparative performance claims are stated as conclusions without numbers: 'an overall improvement in sensitivity and specificity is found for CEUS over CECT', 'CEUS is superior to CT and equivalent to MR imaging', 'CEUS has been shown to be the most cost effective imaging modality in some countries in Europe'. No sensitivity, specificity, confidence interval or cost figure appears for any of these, each resting on block citations

The 80-90% sensitivity for metastasis detection is given as 'up to', i.e. the top of a range whose bottom is not stated, and the claim of particular usefulness for metastases 10 mm or smaller rests on two citations - against Niekel's meta-analysis in this depot, which found per-lesion sensitivity below 10 mm of 47% for CT and 60% for MRI and excluded ultrasound from consideration as rarely used

CEUS is operator-dependent in a way the document acknowledges only through a training recommendation at LoE 5. No interobserver agreement figure appears anywhere, although Chernyak 2018 in this depot reports CEUS LI-RADS category agreement at kappa 0.30-0.39 - the lowest of any modality. A guideline recommending CEUS first-line should report the reproducibility of the test it is recommending

Recommendation 7 advises against routine CEUS for HCC surveillance at LoE 4 with a strong recommendation - the one place the guideline restricts its own modality, and it does so from weak evidence too, which at least shows the grading discordance is not purely self-serving

Four agents with different pharmacokinetics are covered under common recommendations, with regional availability varying; a pathway cannot tell from a given recommendation whether it holds for the agent locally licensed
No expiry date or update interval is stated beyond the pattern of iterations (2004, 2008, 2012, 2020), and the search underlying the 2020 text closed by the June 2019 Granada meeting
32707595.bottom_line: The WFUMB/EFSUMB CEUS liver guidelines, whose single LoE 1 strong recommendation is that CEUS be first-line for an incidentally detected indeterminate focal liver lesion in a non-cirrhotic liver without suspicion of malignancy - it establishes a clear and widely endorsed position for exactly the scenario a pathway must handle, and it establishes almost nothing by its own evidence: no search strategy, no published evidence tables, no accuracy figures or intervals for any comparative claim, several LoE 5 recommendations graded strong, a weaker grade for the higher-risk scenario than the lower, and contrast- and scanner-industry relationships declared by more than twenty of its authors.

critique: The two prevalence figures in the Introduction are the familiar denominator problem in its most compressed form. 'At least one lesion seen in up to 15% of patients' is Kaltenbach's hospital ultrasound population counting five pre-specified benign findings of which 80% were focal fatty sparing and simple cysts; 'benign lesions in nearly 30% of patients with primary malignancy' comes from a different population with a different lesion definition. Both are single-citation, single-number claims with no population described, placed in adjacent sentences as if commensurable, in the opening paragraph that frames every rating that follows

The specificity range cited for contrast-enhanced CT in lesions detected on grayscale ultrasound is 38-82%, and for MRI one cited study gives specificity 43% for an exact diagnosis. A test with specificity that may be below 50% is nonetheless rated Usually Appropriate as an equivalent alternative. The document reports the range and the rating without reconciling them, and a pathway that reads only the rating table never sees the 38%

Declaring CEUS, multiphase CT and contrast-enhanced MRI 'equivalent alternatives' in Variants 1 and 5 is a strong claim resting on narrative accuracy ranges from different studies in different populations, with no head-to-head data, no pooled estimates and no formal equivalence testing. The ranges actually cited (CECT accuracy 74-95%, definitive diagnosis in 71%) are wide enough to encompass clinically important differences

The RAND/UCLA method produces a median rating from a panel and the appropriateness category is a function of that median. For Variant 2 the panel's dispersion forced a special 'Disagreement' label with the admission of insufficient literature - which is the honest case. The other seven variants report no dispersion information at all in the paper, so the reader cannot tell which other ratings were near-unanimous and which were marginal. The final rating-round tabulations exist but are on a separate website, not in the publication

Several procedures are rated Usually Not Appropriate on the explicit basis that 'there is no relevant literature to support the use' - absence of evidence converted into a numerical rating of 1-3. That may be reasonable stewardship but it is not an evidence-based rating, and the document does not distinguish ratings grounded in evidence of no benefit from ratings grounded in no evidence

The risk categories are redefined relative to the ACR white paper in the same family of documents: low and average risk are merged, and high risk is split into liver disease versus extrahepatic malignancy. The change is stated and justified only as being 'for purposes of increased clarity'. A pathway using both ACR documents therefore has to reconcile two incompatible risk taxonomies from the same organisation

The 1 cm boundary separating Variants 1-5 from Variants 6-8 is inherited without derivation, and the document offers no accuracy data stratified by size - despite the entire variant structure resting on that cut-point and despite Niekel's meta-analysis showing per-lesion sensitivity for sub-centimetre lesions of 47% for CT and 60% for MRI

Biopsy drifts from Usually Not Appropriate to May Be Appropriate across variants with no quantified harm or yield anywhere in the document - no complication rate, no diagnostic yield, no seeding risk - so the pathway is given a direction of travel with no magnitudes to weigh

No GRADE certainty rating is attached to any individual recommendation in the published text, despite GRADE being named in the abstract as one of the methodologies. The strength-of-evidence assessment is on the website; what the reader of the paper gets is an appropriateness category

The panel is 18 members, predominantly radiologists, with single representatives from the AGA, the American College of Surgeons and the American College of Physicians. No hepatologist appears in the author affiliations as such, no pathologist, no patient representative and no health economist, in a document that ranks relative radiation level and therefore implicitly trades harm against yield

The relative radiation level scale is given in ordinal pictograms with dose ranges but no attempt to integrate radiation harm with diagnostic benefit; CT with contrast multiphase is 1-10 mSv and is repeatedly rated equivalent to a zero-dose alternative without the equivalence being qualified by that difference

Panel members declare industry relationships including grants from NIDDK, NCI and nine pharmaceutical companies plus Siemens Healthineers, personal fees from MedPace, ICON and Corcept (Dr Bashir), and advisory board attendance for Perspectum Diagnostics (Dr Horowitz)

The document is reviewed annually in principle but carries no expiry date in the text, and its evidence base closes before the CEUS LI-RADS validation work and the 2022 IPD meta-analysis that are also in this depot

The authors note that classifying atypical HCC as LR-M may not be clinically problematic because LI-RADS recommends biopsy of such lesions - an argument that mitigates rather than removes the finding
critique: The headline number is not a pooled estimate. '94% of CEUS LR-M lesions were malignancies' is 54% plus 40%, two independently pooled random-effects proportions from samples with different heterogeneity (I-squared 84% and 88%) added together. The correct figure from the raw counts is 1011/1046 = 96.7%; the correct pooled figure was never computed; and no interval is attached to the 94% anywhere in the paper, including in the abstract, the Key Points, the conclusion and the title-page summary where it appears four times

Removing one case-control study moves the HCC proportion from 54% to 59% and halves I-squared from 84% to 44%. A single study with that much leverage means the primary analysis is driven by study design, not biology, and the authors report the sensitivity analysis in a supplementary figure while keeping 54% as the headline

The Chen et al. case-control study contributes 138 of 1046 LR-M observations, all 100 of its non-HCC malignancies being intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma selected by design. A case-control diagnostic study fixes the malignancy mix by investigator choice, so including it does not estimate a proportion of anything

The forest plot for marked washout reports Makoyeva et al. as 0.28 (95% CI 0.10-1.53). A proportion cannot exceed 1.0; this is an impossible confidence interval printed in a published figure, and it sits inside the pooled 42% estimate that the paper reports as a finding

Two of the 12 studies are conference abstracts (Lyshchik, Ding) contributing 11 and 68 LR-M observations with no peer-reviewed methods; Ding reports no sex distribution and both are among the studies the authors mark at high or unclear risk for flow and timing

Three of the 12 studies (Li, Zhou, Ding) specify none of their non-HCC malignancy diagnoses - 134 of 432 non-HCC malignancies, 31% of the numerator for the key estimate, are uncharacterised. Likewise 27 of 35 benign LR-M lesions are unspecified. The paper's central claim about what LR-M contains therefore has a third of its contents unknown

Zhou et al. is classified as prospective here and the single prospective design subgroup (3 studies) shows no difference from retrospective - but with only 3 prospective studies the design meta-regression has essentially no power, and a non-significant p=0.735 is reported as though it were evidence of no difference

Nation of publication and dominant aetiology return identical point estimates, identical intervals and identical p-values (0.035) in the meta-regression table, because they are the same variable entered twice. The paper reports them as two independent significant moderators, which inflates the apparent number of explanatory findings

The denominator for every estimate is observations in patients at high risk for HCC, mostly HBV-related. The paper's own meta-regression shows the non-HCC malignancy proportion nearly doubling between Asian and Western populations, which is a direct demonstration that these proportions are prevalence-dependent and cannot be applied to a lesion found incidentally in a normal liver

Heterogeneity for the imaging features is 88-95%, yet the frequencies (79%, 42%, 30%) are quoted as feature characteristics. The marked-washout estimate ranges across contributing studies from 13% to 81% - a sixfold spread - and is pooled to 42% (21-64), an interval too wide to distinguish a feature that is usually present from one that is usually absent

Flow and timing was at high or unclear risk of bias in 75% of studies, meaning the interval between CEUS and the reference standard was unknown or inconsistent in most of the dataset. A lesion's category and its final diagnosis may be separated by an unknown time during which it changed, and no sensitivity analysis by this domain was done; the QUADAS-2 covariate entered into meta-regression was patient selection only

Only English-language studies, in a literature where the majority of CEUS LR-M observations come from Chinese centres - the same inconsistency as in Qin et al., and the two reviews share 8 of their included studies while being published five months apart, so they are not independent

The comparison to CT/MRI LR-M (54% vs 22-36% HCC) is across reviews with different inclusion criteria, different reference standards and different populations - an indirect comparison presented without any formal test or caution
34289649.n: 12 studies (10 articles, 2 conference abstracts) with 5728 observations, of which 1046 were LR-M; 7 articles for the imaging-feature analysis
34289649.bottom_line: Pooling 1046 CEUS LR-M observations from 12 studies in high-risk patients, roughly 54% were HCC and 40% non-HCC malignancy, with early washout the commonest feature of non-HCC malignancy at 79% - it establishes that a CEUS LR-M call is a call of malignancy rather than of non-HCC malignancy, and it does not establish the oft-quoted '94% malignant' figure, which is the arithmetic sum of two separately pooled proportions with no confidence interval.

limitations: Less than half of the eligible data sets were made available, which precluded more detailed analysis; the authors recommend clinicians continue to use the current version of LI-RADS until a future iteration is released
Threshold growth was not reported for most observations, and it remains unclear whether its predictive value would differ at centres that routinely repeat CT/MRI within 6-month intervals
Ancillary features were not included because they were incompletely reported in most studies
Extracellular versus hepatobiliary contrast agents could not be compared, because only one study made a direct within-observation comparison and the dataset was skewed toward extracellular agents
Only 12 months of stability was required to establish benignity; a longer interval would have been more specific at the expense of sensitivity

Prolonged interval between index test and reference standard was frequent, although the optimal interval remains uncertain; verification bias from sampling only a subset of observations is another frequent source, since lower-risk observations are less likely to have histological proof
critique: The abstract and Table 3 report threshold growth as OR 1.6 (0.8-3.4), p=.19, while the Discussion reports the same quantity as OR 1.6 (0.7-3.6), p=.07. The paper's single most quoted conclusion - that threshold growth has no association with HCC - is supported by two different confidence intervals and two p-values straddling a conventional threshold, in the same article. A correction notice on the paper ('An earlier incorrect version appeared online. This article was corrected on February 2, 2023') indicates the numbers were not stable at publication

The odds ratios are wildly unstable across the three analysis cohorts, and the paper reports whichever is largest. Nonrim APHE is OR 3.4 at n=452, 14.5 at n=3547 and 10.3 at n=4434. Size >=20 mm is OR 9.7 (p=.01) at n=452, then 0.7 (p=.07) at n=3547, then 1.6 (p=.06) at n=4434 - the point estimate moves from a nearly tenfold increase in odds to a decrease and back. The CT-versus-MRI size comparisons invert similarly (<10 mm: 3.9, then 0.9, then 1.2; >=20 mm: 0.1, then 6.2, then 3.1). Estimates that flip direction with cohort selection are not measuring a stable association, and the authors explain this only as 'interstudy variability'

Enhancing capsule reaches significance in exactly one of three cohorts - OR 2.0 (p=.09) at n=452, 1.3 (p=.08) at n=3547, 2.4 (p=.03) at n=4434. The abstract reports only the significant version. The cohort in which it becomes significant is the largest precisely because it relaxes the requirement that all features be reported, so the significant result comes from the most selectively reported data

The p-values do not correspond to the confidence intervals. OR 13.2 with a 95% CI of 9.0-19.2 is reported as p=.01, and OR 2.4 with CI 1.7-3.5 also as p=.03; an interval excluding 1.0 by that margin corresponds to p values many orders of magnitude smaller. The p-values appear to be floored or mis-transcribed, which means the paper's inferential statements cannot be checked against its own estimates

Only 32 of 81 eligible studies contributed data - 40% - and participation was by author willingness. Which studies share data is not random: authors with clean, complete, favourable datasets are likelier to agree. The IPD design buys granularity at the cost of a severe and unmeasured selection on study provenance, and the paper's own list of non-responders is relegated to an online appendix

78% of studies were at high risk of bias, and the CEUS sensitivity analysis - the arm whose conclusions are newest and least corroborated - could not be performed at all because only 2 CEUS studies were at low risk and the model would not converge. Every CEUS conclusion in the paper therefore rests on data the authors could not stress-test

CEUS rests on 853 observations from 6 studies, with each feature's OR estimated from a subset of those. A finding like 'marked washout was not associated with diagnosis or nondiagnosis of HCC (OR 0.7, 0.2-2.8)' is an interval spanning a fivefold decrease to a near-threefold increase - uninformative rather than null, which the paper reports as a conclusion

Threshold growth's non-association is confounded with its missingness. It was assessable in only 452 of 4434 observations (10%), missing mostly because prior imaging did not exist. Observations with prior imaging available are those under surveillance - a different population from those presenting de novo - so the one cohort that could test threshold growth is the least representative. The paper states this and still frames the result as 'threshold growth is not a significant predictor'

Definitions were pooled across five LI-RADS versions (CT/MRI v2014, v2017, v2018; CEUS v2016, v2017) in which threshold growth itself was redefined - v2018 requires >=50% in <=6 months while v2014/v2017 also allowed >=100% beyond 6 months and new >=10 mm observations within 24 months. The authors state the specific criterion applied could not be retrospectively identified, so the variable being modelled has no single definition

Where multiple readers existed, data from one reader was chosen at random in 6 studies; in one study the less-represented contrast agent was deliberately preferred to improve representation. These are reasonable choices but they are analyst decisions made after seeing the data, with no pre-specification in the protocol and no sensitivity analysis

Benignity required only 12 months of imaging stability for 412 of 1373 benign observations (30%), and the authors concede a longer interval would be more specific. Well-differentiated HCC can be stable for longer than a year, so some HCCs sit in the benign reference group, biasing every OR toward 1

Primary-study investigators were contacted to resolve unclear or inconsistent data in 9 studies - i.e. the IPD did not match the published reports in more than a quarter of contributing studies, which is a provenance concern the paper notes neutrally

Four of 32 studies are conference abstracts. Several authors carry substantial imaging-industry relationships and the chair of the LI-RADS Steering Committee is a co-author on a paper evaluating LI-RADS's own feature set

As with every paper in this group, the denominator is patients at high risk for HCC. An odds ratio for a feature is not a probability, and these ORs cannot be converted into a post-test probability for a lesion found incidentally in a normal liver without a prevalence the paper does not supply
34783596.n: 32 studies (28 articles, 4 conference abstracts); 1170 CT observations in 812 patients from 6 studies, 3341 MRI observations in 2639 patients from 17 studies, 853 CEUS observations in 833 patients from 6 studies; 813 observations had both CT and MRI
34783596.bottom_line: Pooling observation-level data on 5364 observations from 32 studies in high-risk patients, washout and arterial phase hyperenhancement are the features that carry LI-RADS, enhancing capsule contributes weakly and threshold growth not at all - it establishes that the major features are not equivalent and should not be weighted equally, and it does not establish stable effect sizes for any of them, given odds ratios that invert direction between analysis cohorts and a threshold-growth result reported with two different intervals in one paper.

limitations: No limitations section - the paper has no section acknowledging its own limitations, and the discussion closes with the conclusion restated
The authors do note that reasons for the lower LR-3 HCC risk in Asian populations 'requires further study to confirm', speculating about hepatitis B as the dominant risk factor
They note the revision of CEUS LR-M criteria needs more evidence-based studies
They note that the significance of LR-M for diagnosing overall malignancy and the key indicators still need further exploration
critique: Ten studies, of which one is prospective and one (Stepan et al.) is a conference abstract published only as a journal supplement page with no patient number, age or sex reported. Two studies - Zheng (2020 observations) and Li (1366 observations) - contribute 55% of all lesions, so the pooled estimates are effectively those two Chinese cohorts

The denominator is patients at high risk for HCC, overwhelmingly with hepatitis B (the two dominant studies are HBV cohorts). Every proportion is a positive predictive value under that prevalence and cannot be carried into a non-cirrhotic incidental lesion. The paper itself demonstrates the prevalence sensitivity by showing the LR-3 HCC proportion moving from 14% to 33% between Asian and non-Asian populations, then does not draw the obvious inference about transportability

Heterogeneity is extreme and unaddressed: I-squared 86% for LR-3, 89% for LR-4, 92% for LR-M, and 95-98% for LR-5 sensitivity, specificity and accuracy. Pooling an accuracy estimate with I-squared 98% produces a number with no population referent, and the paper reports it to two decimal places (0.82) and uses it in its conclusion

Table 3 and the results text disagree on LR-M accuracy (0.91 vs 90%) and badly on LR-M DOR (50.9, 95% CI 19.90-130.43 vs 45.7, 95% CI 22.1-94.5). One of these pairs is wrong and the paper does not say which

The paper's most actionable claim - that multidisciplinary discussion may be unnecessary for CEUS LR-3 - rests on a point estimate of 21% (95% CI 13-33%) whose upper bound is a one-in-three chance of HCC, and on a meta-regression showing the estimate depends on region and version. A 13-33% interval does not license dropping a safeguard, and the authors offer no decision-analytic basis for the claim

The v2016-versus-v2017 difference in LR-3 HCC proportion (46% vs 15%) occurs even though the authors state the LR-3 criteria did not change between versions. That is a signal that the difference is confounded by which populations adopted which version, not a version effect - the authors say as much and then still report it as a version comparison

Averaging data across readers within a study ('if more than one data set was available, the data were averaged') destroys all information about interobserver agreement in a modality where category assignment is known to be only fairly reproducible

Reference standard is mixed within and across studies, and the meta-regression shows it matters: LR-5 specificity 87% with pathology versus 96% with a composite standard. Composite standards incorporate imaging into the reference, inflating apparent specificity. The pooled 95% specificity therefore sits closer to the inflated end, and the paper presents it as the headline

Only English-language publications were eligible, in a field where much of the CEUS literature is Chinese-language - an odd restriction given that the authors' own meta-regression identifies region as the dominant source of heterogeneity

Publication bias was not assessed at all, on the authority of a guidance document; no funnel plot, no Egger test, no discussion of small-study effects in a literature dominated by two large cohorts and eight small ones

The study overlaps heavily with Zhou et al. 2022 from the same Tianjin department, published two months later in Frontiers in Oncology, with shared authors (Qin, Zhou, Ding, Chen, Jing), overlapping included studies and the same funding. A pathway citing both as independent corroboration is double-counting one body of work
QUADAS-2 results are relegated to supplementary material and no sensitivity analysis by risk of bias is performed, despite the reference-standard domain demonstrably driving the specificity estimate

Table 1's study characteristics contain an error of provenance - Ghiuchici et al. 2021 is listed as 'Korea' when the study is Romanian (Timisoara) - which raises doubt about the region variable on which the headline meta-regression depends
35164930.n: 10 included studies (1 prospective, 9 retrospective), 5543 patients with 6124 lesions including 4492 HCCs, 476 non-HCC malignancies and 1156 benign lesions
35164930.bottom_line: Pooling 6124 lesions from 10 mostly retrospective, mostly Asian CEUS studies in high-risk patients, the HCC proportion rises from 2% at LR-2 to 97% at LR-5 with LR-3 only about 21% and LR-M 44% HCC - it establishes that CEUS LR-3 carries a lower HCC risk than the figure on which current management guidance was built, and it does not establish a stable estimate for any category, given I-squared values of 83-98%, near-total dependence on two Chinese HBV cohorts, and an unreconciled region effect.

limitations: Few paired studies were available, so the central CEUS-versus-CT/MRI comparison is mostly indirect, between different study populations rather than within patients
The heterogeneity of the distribution and diagnostic performance of HCC could not be well explained by meta-regression
The effect of tumour size on LI-RADS classification was not explored
critique: Table 4 (LR-M for non-HCC malignancy) reproduces the specificity, accuracy, I-squared and p-value rows of Table 3 (LR-5 for HCC) verbatim: specificity 92% vs 92% with I-squared 75 and 86 and p=0.96, accuracy 78% vs 76% with I-squared 90 and 93 and p=0.54. It is not credible that two different index tests for two different targets produced identical estimates to the percentage point and identical I-squared values. The LR-M specificity and accuracy figures are a copy error, which means the paper's own table cannot support any statement about LR-M specificity - yet the abstract and conclusion both trade on LR-M performance

The meta-regression reports CEUS LR-M sensitivity for non-HCC malignancy as 60.0% with pathology and 69.0% with a composite standard, both far below the pooled 83% reported in Table 4 and the abstract. Two incompatible sets of numbers for the same quantity appear in the same paper, and neither is reconciled

'A total of 43 studies were included' but 15 CEUS plus 30 CT/MRI studies is 45. Two studies presumably contributed to both arms, which would make the headline CEUS-versus-CT/MRI comparison partly within-study and partly between-study, but the paper never identifies them or accounts for the correlation

The first HIGHLIGHTS bullet reads 'CEUS LR-3 has a lower proportion of HCCs than CT/MRI LR-M' where the body of the paper compares LR-3 with LR-3. A reader taking the highlights at face value imports a comparison the study never made

The denominator throughout is lesions in patients at high risk for HCC - cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B - with SonoVue. Every proportion is a positive predictive value under high HCC prevalence. The paper's own meta-regression shows the LR-3 HCC proportion moving from 14% to 32% by region, which is a demonstration that these figures are population artefacts, yet the conclusions are stated as properties of the categories

The CEUS-versus-CT/MRI comparison that the paper exists to make is acknowledged as mostly indirect because few paired studies exist. Comparing proportions across populations with different HCC prevalence, different aetiology and different reference standards, then attaching p-values to the differences, is a between-study comparison dressed as a head-to-head test - the significant LR-3 (p=0.02) and LR-M (p=0.01) differences are the most likely casualties

Heterogeneity of 78-93% for the proportions and 75-96% for the performance estimates, which the authors concede meta-regression could not explain. A DOR pooled with I-squared 96% (CEUS LR-M, 36.5, 95% CI 16.6-80.0) has no interpretable referent

The reference-standard meta-regression result is the opposite of the usual direction and is left unexamined: CT/MRI LR-4 and LR-5 contained FEWER HCCs when pathology was the standard (63.4% vs 81.2%; 92.3% vs 97%). Composite standards that confirm HCC by LR-5 appearance on another modality are incorporation bias, and this result quantifies it - roughly 5 to 18 percentage points of the headline LR-5 and LR-4 figures. The paper reports it and then uses the pooled (inflated) values in its conclusions

The v2017-versus-v2018 difference for CT/MRI LR-M HCC proportion is 6% versus 42.2% (p=0.04), a sevenfold swing attributed to a version change. Pooling across versions when the version effect is that large makes the single pooled LR-M estimate of 33% an average over incompatible definitions

Substantial overlap with Qin et al. 2022 from the same department, same funding grants, overlapping authors (Zhou, Qin, Ding, Chen, Jing) and overlapping included CEUS studies, published two months apart. The two papers report different CEUS LR-M HCC proportions (56% here, 44% in Qin) from largely the same primary literature without either acknowledging the other's estimate. A pathway citing both as corroborating evidence is counting one dataset twice and importing an unexplained 12-point discrepancy

Data from multiple readers within a study were averaged, discarding interobserver variability, and the authors state 'no discrepancy was found' between the two data extractors - an implausible claim across 43 studies that suggests extraction was not genuinely independent
English-only inclusion, publication bias not assessed by any method, QUADAS-2 results confined to supplementary material with no sensitivity analysis by risk of bias
Non-HCC malignancy numerators are small for several categories (CEUS LR-TIV 3% of 100 observations, CT/MRI LR-TIV 22% of 102) yet are reported as proportions with intervals and compared with p-values
35425706.n: 43 studies included; 15 CEUS studies with 6573 patients and 7234 lesions (5387 HCC, 624 non-HCC malignancy, 1223 benign) and 30 CT/MRI studies with 5274 patients and 6522 lesions (4554 HCC, 481 non-HCC malignancy, 1487 benign)
35425706.bottom_line: Pooling 43 studies in high-risk patients, corresponding CEUS and CT/MRI LI-RADS categories carry similar HCC risk except LR-3 (21% vs 35%) and LR-M (56% vs 33% HCC), and LR-5 performs equivalently in both systems - it establishes that the two systems are not interchangeable at LR-3 and LR-M, and it cannot establish anything reliable about LR-M specificity or accuracy, because those table rows are duplicated from the LR-5 analysis.

limitations: Despite 28 articles, the study may be underpowered for some comparisons - the authors name B-HCA vs I-HCA specifically - reflecting the rarity of some subtypes
All 16 case reports and case series were judged high risk of bias in the patient selection domain, and some original investigations also had high risk of bias or high applicability concern

The outcome was a dichotomous qualitative assessment of HBP signal, which may be affected by lesion size and internal heterogeneity; only one of 28 articles stated how heterogeneous lesions were classified (iso-/hyperintense if present in at least 25% of the lesion), and the reference tissue for the qualitative comparison was unspecified in 12 of 28 articles

Cited external evidence that enhancement pattern matters and was not captured: 93% of FNHs show homogeneous HBP hyperintensity whereas 70% of HBP iso-/hyperintense HCAs are heterogeneous, and apparent HBP iso-/hyperintensity may not reflect true uptake when background liver is steatotic
Additional subtypes from the 2017 classification (exon 3-mutated B-HCA, exon 7/8-mutated B-HCA, sonic hedgehog HCA) were not evaluated because of a paucity of literature

Four of the 12 original investigations had high risk of bias from a case-control design for FNH-versus-HCA differentiation; one incorporated the index test into the FNH reference standard; one established some FNH diagnoses by MRI stability despite HCA also being capable of stability
critique: Sixteen of 28 included studies are case reports and case series, and they are the dominant source of the B-HCA signal. A case report of a beta-catenin adenoma gets written precisely because it was HBP hyperintense and therefore surprised someone; pooling such reports with cohort data does not estimate a proportion, it estimates reportability. The 59% for B-HCA is the output of that circularity, and the authors' own sensitivity analysis excluding case reports is absent

The B-HCA estimate rests on 33 lesions spread across studies, with a 95% interval of 26-88%. A pathway cannot act differently at 26% than at 88%, so the interval, not the point estimate, is the finding - yet the abstract, the Key Finding box, the Clinical Impact box and the conclusion all repeat '59%'

A sensitivity of 99% with a 95% CI of 57-100% is not a measurement. The lower bound is barely better than a coin toss, and it is reported four separate times in the paper as '99%' without the interval. The same applies to the 99% (53-100%) for B-HCA/U-HCA

The entire secondary objective rests on 4 studies, all drawn from the primary set, and the authors' own QUADAS-2 assessment marks all four as high risk of bias for patient selection because they are case-control in design. Case-control diagnostic studies fix the ratio of FNH to HCA by investigator choice, so the specificity figures of 89% and 65% are functions of the sampling and not of the test

The specificity drop from 89% to 65% is produced by *removing* H-HCA and I-HCA from the comparison - i.e. by changing the spectrum of the disease group, not by any change in the test. The paper frames this as revealing the true specificity, but it is the specificity against an artificially enriched population that would arise only after conventional MRI has already excluded the two subtypes with characteristic features. The pathway-relevant question - specificity in an unselected lesion before subtyping - is 89%, and the paper does not say so plainly

The B-HCA-versus-I-HCA pairwise comparison came out at exactly the Bonferroni threshold (p=.008) and is marked non-significant. Since I-HCA is the commonest subtype (203 of 410 lesions) and also carries beta-catenin mutations in 10-20% of cases, the failure to separate it from B-HCA undermines the clinical use of HBP signal as a malignancy surrogate - a conclusion the paper gestures at but does not draw

Heterogeneity was substantial where it matters most: I-squared 83% for I-HCA and 74% overall. With 12 cohort studies and 16 case reports, no metaregression on study type was performed, so the contribution of the case-report literature to that heterogeneity is unquantified

The outcome is operator-dependent and inconsistently defined across studies: the reference tissue was unspecified in 12 of 28 articles, only 1 of 28 defined how to score a heterogeneous lesion, and no interobserver agreement is reported anywhere. Pooling a binary read whose definition varies by study produces a number with no fixed meaning

Three of the included studies also performed quantitative HBP assessment and the authors acknowledge an external finding that 70% of HBP-positive HCAs are heterogeneous while 93% of FNHs are homogeneous - i.e. the feature that would fix the specificity problem was available and excluded by the protocol's dichotomous outcome definition

The subtype denominators are discordant with the subtype epidemiology the paper itself quotes in its introduction (H-HCA 30-40%, I-HCA 40-55%, B-HCA 10-20%, U-HCA 5-10%): the included sample is 27% H-HCA, 50% I-HCA, 8% B-HCA, 15% U-HCA. B-HCA is under-represented relative to its expected frequency even before considering the case-report enrichment, so the overall 14% figure is not a population-weighted estimate

One included study (Agarwal) contributed 24 I-HCAs of which 17 were never biopsied - they were called I-HCA because they looked identical on the same gadoxetic acid MRI being evaluated. That is direct incorporation bias in the largest I-HCA contributor after Auer, flagged in QUADAS-2 but retained in the pooled estimate with no sensitivity analysis

Senior author declares consultancy to Bayer Healthcare, the manufacturer of gadoxetic acid (Eovist/Primovist), in a paper whose conclusion restricts the clinical use of that agent - a conflict that cuts against the finding and so is less troubling, but it is unmentioned in the discussion
35920706.n: 28 studies (12 original investigations, 16 case reports or case series), 364 patients with 410 HCAs (112 H-HCA, 203 I-HCA, 33 B-HCA, 62 U-HCA); 4 studies with 150 FNHs and 137 HCAs for the diagnostic-performance analysis
35920706.bottom_line: Pooling 410 subtyped adenomas from 12 cohort studies and 16 case reports, HBP iso- or hyperintensity occurs in 0% of HNF1A-inactivated but 59% (95% CI 26-88%) of beta-catenin-activated adenomas, and specificity for FNH falls from 89% to 65% once H-HCA and I-HCA are excluded - it establishes that HBP signal alone cannot be used to call a lesion FNH, and it does not establish a reliable proportion for any individual subtype, resting as it does on 33 B-HCAs drawn largely from case reports.
