limitations: The most important limitation stated is the composite imaging-and-histology reference standard; the authors argue histology for every HCC is no longer standard of care and so is practically impossible to obtain

Observations with persistent CT/MRI LR-3 at 1-year follow-up were counted as non-malignant, but the authors acknowledge that the growth rate of some well-differentiated HCC means 1 year may not be long enough to exclude malignancy, and conversely that nodules called non-malignant may transform later
CEUS readers were not blinded to the CT/MRI images or results in most cases, as in routine practice where CT/MRI guides the CEUS examination, which the authors argue increases clinical applicability
Despite the prospective multicentre design, the relatively small sample size of 75 liver lesions in this sub-analysis may affect generalisability and statistical power
critique: The population is 97.1% cirrhotic patients at risk for HCC, 23.5% with a personal history of HCC, enrolled because they already had a focal liver lesion on surveillance. This licenses nothing about an incidental mass in a normal liver. The study's own numbers make the point: at this prevalence, CT/MRI LR-3 carried a 26% HCC risk - in a non-cirrhotic liver the same imaging appearance carries a far lower risk and CEUS LR-5 would no longer have a 100% positive predictive value

The headline 'PPV 100%, NPV 100%' figures come from 7, 7, 1 and 6 observations respectively. A PPV of 7/7 has an exact 95% confidence interval of roughly 59-100%; an NPV of 1/1 is uninformative. No confidence interval appears anywhere in the paper for any of these proportions, and they are stated as '100%' in the abstract, results, discussion and conclusion

The denominator shrinks from 646 enrolled patients to 68, and from an unstated number of observations to 75, by a selection that is partly on the reference standard: observations that were LR-4 on 1-year follow-up were excluded for uncertainty, and LR-M/LR-TIV without histology were excluded. Excluding the hardest cases from a study of how to resolve hard cases inflates the apparent resolution rate, and the paper reports no flow diagram or count of exclusions

Readers were not blinded to the CT/MRI result. Since the index test is a subjective category assignment and the comparator is the CT/MRI category being superseded, unblinding allows the CEUS reader to move a lesion in the direction clinical suspicion already points. The authors defend this as clinical realism, which it is, but it means the study measures the performance of CEUS-plus-prior-knowledge, not of CEUS

The reference standard is CT/MRI follow-up in 54 of 75 observations (72%) - the same modality whose indeterminacy CEUS is being credited with resolving. A lesion downgraded by CEUS and then confirmed benign by stable CT/MRI is confirmed by the test that could not characterise it in the first place. This is incorporation bias in the direction of the study's conclusion, and the single incorrect re-categorisation was itself resolved by follow-up MRI rather than the recommended biopsy

Counting a persistently LR-3 observation at 1 year as 'non-malignant' is a definitional choice that assigns the ambiguous cases to the benign column. The authors flag it; the arithmetic consequence - that the 72.2% non-malignant rate in LR-3 includes nodules of genuinely unknown status - is not quantified

'Management recommendation changed in 33.3% and was correct in 96%' conflates two different things. Of the 25 changes, 21 were to a definitive category and 4 prompted a biopsy or workup; the 96% correctness is computed over all 25 including those where 'correct' means 'biopsy was appropriately recommended'. The clinically useful figure - follow-up imaging genuinely avoided - is 21/75 (28%), i.e. CEUS left 72% of indeterminate observations still indeterminate

Three of 75 observations became LR-NC on CEUS, a fact reported only in passing. CEUS therefore created new non-characterizable observations in the LR-3 group while eliminating them in the LR-NC group, and the net effect on the volume of unresolved findings is never computed

This is a sub-analysis of a trial designed and powered for a different question (validation of CEUS LI-RADS overall, reported separately in Hepatology 2024). The subgroup was not the basis of the sample size calculation, no power analysis is given for it, and the authors acknowledge the sample size limits generalisability - yet the conclusion is a practice recommendation that 'CEUS should be strongly considered as an appropriate next step'

Eleven academic and non-academic sites with CEUS examiners of 3-25 years' experience, on-site application support, educational materials and a pictorial essay from the ACR working group. This is a best-case operator environment; no interobserver agreement is reported and no estimate is offered of how the result would degrade in a centre without that support

Funded in part by Bracco Diagnostics, the manufacturer of the contrast agent used (Lumason/SonoVue), in a study concluding that the agent should be used more. Sixteen of the 18 authors declare relationships with ultrasound-equipment or contrast manufacturers, including Bracco advisory board membership, consulting agreements and research support for the senior and corresponding authors. The comparator - repeat CT/MRI - is the product the funder does not sell
Cirrhosis was biopsy-proven in only 7.4% of the cohort, so the defining inclusion characteristic is itself largely a clinical-radiological judgement
38860996.n: 75 observations in 68 patients (54 LR-3, 21 LR-NC), drawn from 646 enrolled patients
38860996.bottom_line: In a prospective multicentre cohort of 75 CT/MRI-indeterminate observations in 68 patients who were 97% cirrhotic, CEUS resolved a third of them and changed management correctly in 24 of 25 cases - it establishes, in patients at risk for HCC and with readers who could see the prior CT/MRI, that CEUS is a reasonable next step for an LR-3 or LR-NC nodule; it does not establish any performance figure with usable precision (the 100% PPV and NPV rest on 7, 7, 6 and 1 observations), and it licenses nothing at all about an incidental mass in a non-cirrhotic liver.
38860996.funding: NIH/NCI R01 CA215520 and Bracco Diagnostics; A. Singal's research supported in part by NCI U01 CA283935. Extensive author disclosures with Bracco, GE HealthCare, Philips, Siemens, Canon, Samsung, Lantheus and others

limitations: The author attributes the much higher rates than prior literature (haemangioma 0.35-7%, bile duct tumours 0.6-2.8%, FNH 1-2%) to detection: small lesions are overlooked at routine non-targeted autopsy, so the 52% reflects search intensity as much as biology
Lesion sizes were far smaller than in surgical series (FNH 0.8 cm here vs 5.6 cm reported by Gold et al; adenoma 0.6 cm vs 7.5 cm), implicitly conceding these are not the lesions clinicians see
Drug history was unavailable for the peliosis case and no hospitalisation records were obtainable
No patient had a history of sex hormone treatment, limiting inference about hormonal aetiology
critique: The denominator is 95 forensic autopsies in Finnish men only - no women, no one under 35 or over 69. Any pathway quoting '52% prevalence of benign liver lesions' as a general-population figure is extrapolating from 95 dead Finnish men to a mixed-sex clinic population

The population is selected for violent, unexpected or intoxication-related death: 49.5% cardiovascular, 15.8% alcohol/drug intoxication, 17.9% other violent death, and only 1% neoplastic. This is systematically younger, more male and more alcohol-exposed than a radiology population, and the near-absence of cancer deaths means the metastasis denominator is meaningless

The 52% is dominated by lesions that are radiologically invisible: 26 bile duct tumours with a mean diameter of 1.3 mm and 19 haemangiomas with a mean of 5.2 mm. Nothing at 1.3 mm can be seen on CT, so this figure cannot be used to set a prior probability for an incidentally imaged mass

Microhamartomas and bile duct adenomas - biologically distinct entities, one a ductal plate malformation and one a neoplasm - were deliberately pooled into 'bile duct tumours', inflating the single largest contributor to the 52%

Single observer, single centre, no second reader, no blinding for the targeted blocks (only the 285 routine blocks were read blind to the suspect-lesion results), and the targeted blocks are where almost everything was found

Numerators are tiny for the lesions clinicians actually worry about: n=1 adenoma, n=3 FNH, n=1 peliosis. The confidence interval around a 1/95 estimate spans roughly 0-6%, which the paper never states
The statistics are two-tailed t-tests on separate variances across seven lesion types with no correction for multiplicity, yet p-values are reported to three decimals
Funded by the Finnish Foundation of Alcohol Studies, in a series where 15.8% of deaths were alcohol-related - the sampling frame and the funder's interest coincide
3950039.n: 95 consecutive medicolegal autopsies, all men aged 35-69
3950039.bottom_line: In 95 forensic autopsies of Finnish men aged 35-69, half had a benign hepatic lesion, but almost all were millimetre-scale bile duct microhamartomas and small haemangiomas - this establishes that tiny benign lesions are ubiquitous at targeted pathology, and does not establish any prevalence relevant to a radiologically detected incidental mass.
3950039.funding: Supported by a grant from the Finnish Foundation of Alcohol Studies

limitations: No consensus exists on the definition, classification or grading of endoscopic adverse events, and descriptions in the source literature are often neither comprehensive nor detailed
Reporting of adverse events was a minor component of the reviewed articles, hindering reliable data for subgroup comparison
Baseline patient characteristics were not accounted for - age, sex, comorbidities including compensated cirrhosis and end-stage renal disease, and anticoagulant use
Tumour characteristics not considered - size, vascularity, presence of a cystic component
Technical factors not evaluated - sampling route, technique (slow-pull or negative pressure), number of needle passes

The authors note it is challenging to analyse the correlation between patient characteristics and AEs because most studies do not report such information, and that vascular-rich tumours and cirrhosis are identified as risk factors
critique: The abstract concludes 'no associated deaths' while the results report, in the liver subgroup, 'one [patient] with suspected death from discontinuation of anticoagulants'. A death is counted in the numerator of the liver AE rate and then denied in the conclusion. For a pathway considering EUS-FNB of a liver lesion, this is the single most consequential sentence in the paper and it contradicts the data two pages earlier

The liver figure a pathway would actually use - 14.0% - rests on 133 patients in 4 studies with 18 events, and has a 95% confidence interval of 7.7-24.0%. Thirteen of the 18 events are abdominal pain. The clinically serious events are 3 bleeds and 1 death in 133 patients, i.e. 3%, which the paper never states as a figure. Both the alarming headline (14%) and the reassuring headline (1.8% overall) are therefore misleading in opposite directions, and neither is the number that matters

The 'bleeding being the most common AE at 44.0%' in the abstract is a proportion of adverse events, not of patients. The per-patient rate is 0.8%. The abstract gives 1.8% and 44.0% in the same sentence with no indication that the denominators differ by a factor of 56, which invites a reader to conclude that 44% of patients bleed

The denominator is overwhelmingly pancreatic and submucosal: 9303 patients of whom only 133 (1.4%) had liver puncture. A meta-analysis whose title and conclusion are about safety of EUS-FNB is 98.6% about other organs, and the organ with the highest event rate is the one with the least data

The arithmetic does not reconcile. Ninety-nine studies are claimed, but the subgroup analysis counts 31 prospective plus 55 retrospective (86), the RCT count is given as 10 in one place and 13 in another, and the reported study-type breakdown elsewhere in the text names 'four liver biopsy studies' and '11' submucosal studies against 'eleven studies ... in a total of 516 patients'. No PRISMA counts are reconcilable from the text supplied

'P = 0.0.043' is printed in the results for the prospective-versus-retrospective comparison - a typographical failure in the paper's only significant moderator analysis. The finding itself (prospective rates 60% higher than retrospective) is the clearest evidence in the paper that the overall 1.8% is an underestimate from retrospective under-ascertainment, and the conclusion does not incorporate it

The conclusion that EUS-FNB 'is a safe procedure with a relatively low risk' is drawn from a pooled rate dominated by retrospective studies which the paper's own subgroup analysis shows report significantly fewer events. The authors' prior FNA review gave 0.98%; this FNB figure is 1.8%, i.e. roughly double, a comparison the paper makes in the introduction and omits from the conclusion

No risk-of-bias assessment of any kind is described in the available text - no QUADAS, no Newcastle-Ottawa, no Cochrane RoB for the RCT subset - and no sensitivity analysis by study quality, despite pooling RCTs with retrospective series

Heterogeneity statistics are absent for the pooled rates. A proportion pooled across 99 studies with event counts as low as zero needs an I-squared and a model justification; none is reported for the overall estimate, only confidence intervals

The claim that no needle-tract implantation was reported is used to reassure, but the authors themselves note implantation is 'infrequent and delayed' and that the included studies document only short-term AEs. Absence of a long-latency outcome in studies with short follow-up is not evidence of its absence, and no follow-up duration is reported for any subgroup

The two factors the discussion names as risk factors for AEs - vascular-rich tumours and cirrhosis - are precisely the characteristics of the patients in whom a liver lesion would be biopsied, and are also the variables the paper concedes it could not analyse. The 14% liver rate may therefore be either an over- or under-estimate for a cirrhotic patient with a hypervascular lesion, and the direction is unknown

The three negative subgroup findings (needle type, needle diameter, prospective versus retrospective within the pancreas) are all reported as 'no significant difference' on the basis of p-values alone, with no equivalence margin and no power calculation, so absence of evidence is being read as evidence of absence

Publication bias is not assessed - no funnel plot, no Egger test - in a safety literature where adverse events are a secondary outcome that goes unreported in studies designed for diagnostic yield, which the authors concede is exactly what happened
39789825.n: 99 studies, 9303 patients, 166 adverse events; the liver subgroup is 4 studies with 133 patients
39789825.bottom_line: Pooling 99 studies and 9303 patients, 20-22G second-generation EUS-FNB carried an overall adverse event rate of 1.8%, mostly mild bleeding and pancreatitis, but 14.0% (95% CI 7.7-24.0%) at the liver - it establishes that EUS-FNB of a liver lesion carries a materially higher complication rate than of the pancreas, and it does not establish a usable liver figure, resting on 133 patients and 18 events of which 13 were abdominal pain and one was a death the abstract denies occurred.
39789825.funding: Not stated in the available text; no conflict of interest statement located

limitations: The biopsy cohort used for lesion identification was derived exclusively from European centres and included only patients with specific signs of portal hypertension, although samples were independently evaluated by pathologists from multiple regions
Paediatric liver biopsies were not included; extending the histological framework to patients without portal hypertension and to paediatric populations is named as an important next step
Although new scientific data supported several key modifications, other aspects necessarily relied on expert consensus in the absence of conclusive evidence
The diagnostic score was derived from expert opinion rather than prospective validation, which the authors state should be addressed in future studies
Direct application to paediatric patients requires caution because age-specific thresholds for clinical, laboratory and elastographic parameters are not yet defined
No robust data are available to define the biopsy characteristics required to optimally identify the histological lesions of PSVD/NCPF, as opposed to excluding cirrhosis
The authors state the responsibility now lies with the scientific community to generate the data required to validate, refine or modify the score over time
critique: The diagnostic score is validated circularly and the paper says so without flinching: 36 hypothetical scenarios were voted on by the Nomenclature Group, the votes were converted into weighted points, and the resulting score 'reproduced 100% of expert agreement across all voted scenarios'. A score fitted to a panel's votes and then shown to reproduce those votes has been checked for arithmetic consistency, not for diagnostic validity. The Delphi validation (Figure 3) is agreement with the score by a second set of experts, not agreement with any patient outcome. No patient was ever classified by this score in the paper

The 36 scenarios are hypothetical vignettes, not patients. The weights therefore encode what experts believe about combinations of findings, including combinations that may be vanishingly rare or impossible in practice, and the score's performance in a real consecutive series is unknown

The central terminology decision failed its own pre-specified threshold. Consensus was defined a priori as 75% agreement; 'disorder' was selected with 74%. The paper reports both numbers without noting that the headline term in the title did not meet the standard the Methods set, and the rationale offered is conceptual breadth rather than evidence

The lesion-identification cohort is 88 PSVD/NCPF cases from European centres only, all with specific signs of portal hypertension - while Statement 3 (92% agreement) permits diagnosis in patients without portal hypertension. The criteria were therefore derived in one population and are licensed for use in another in which they have never been tested. For an incidental finding, this is the population that matters: a patient with an incidentally noted nodular liver and no portal hypertension is precisely who the criteria were not derived on

The a priori major-criterion threshold of sensitivity >0.10 is extraordinarily permissive. A lesion present in 11% of cases qualifies as a major criterion provided specificity exceeds 0.95. The framework is therefore built for ruling in and is explicitly not built for ruling out, and the consensus does not state the sensitivity of the full criterion set - so the proportion of PSVD/NCPF patients whose biopsy satisfies no criterion is unreported

Specificity was measured against 41 normal donors and 89 chronic liver disease controls that deliberately excluded biliary disease. Biliary disease is excluded from the definition, which makes the exclusion internally consistent, but it means the >0.95 specificity figures were never tested against the differential that a nodular non-cirrhotic liver most often raises in practice

An elementary lesion was counted as present when more than 50% of nine pathologists reported it. No kappa, no intraclass correlation and no per-lesion agreement statistic is given for any of the criteria in the available text, in a consensus whose criteria are entirely histological judgements. Majority voting among nine expert pathologists with a shared atlas is also the best possible case; reproducibility in a general pathology service is unaddressed

The consensus states plainly that the lesions are not pathognomonic and occur in other liver diseases, and that the entity may coexist with other liver diseases provided cirrhosis is excluded. Combined with a sensitivity floor of 0.10 and a score permitting diagnosis without portal hypertension, the definition is broad enough that the boundary with incidental histological change in an otherwise normal or diseased liver is set by expert weighting rather than by data

Nodular regenerative hyperplasia becomes a major criterion for a vascular disorder - a reclassification with direct consequences for any pathway that currently reassures patients about NRH as a benign nodular lesion. The consensus does not address how an NRH diagnosis made on imaging or on a biopsy taken for another reason should be handled, nor what proportion of incidentally detected NRH represents PSVD/NCPF

The biopsy adequacy standard was reduced from 20 mm with 10 portal tracts to 15 mm with one 10 mm fragment on the basis of a single cited reference (14), with 100% panel agreement. The evidence cited addresses excluding cirrhosis only, and the consensus concedes no data define adequacy for identifying PSVD lesions - so the 15 mm standard is validated for the exclusion step and assumed for the inclusion step

Statement 1 makes liver biopsy mandatory (95% agreement) in a disorder that can be diagnosed without portal hypertension, which means the consensus mandates an invasive procedure with the harms quantified in Rockey's AASLD paper for patients who may be entirely asymptomatic. No risk-benefit analysis, no estimate of how many biopsies would be needed to find one case, and no discussion of the harms of biopsying incidentally detected nodularity appears

Consensus statements carry agreement percentages but no evidence grades. Nine of the statements visible in the text report 92-100% agreement, which measures panel cohesion rather than evidence quality - and the paper itself concedes that aspects 'necessarily relied on expert consensus in the absence of conclusive evidence'. High agreement on weak evidence is the recurring pattern across the guidelines in this depot

Several panel members declare industry consultancies including Cook Medical and GORE Medical (a speakers' bureau for the lead author, both makers of devices used in portal hypertension), Mirum, Ipsen, Sarepta, Orchard, PathAI, Perspectum and AstraZeneca

Published 2026 as a 'first internationally endorsed, unified framework' with an explicit handoff of validation to the community; a pathway adopting it is adopting an unvalidated score by the authors' own description
42191146.n: 218 liver biopsies for the histological criteria: 41 normal living-donor samples, 89 chronic liver disease controls (alcohol-associated, MASLD, viral, autoimmune) and 88 PSVD/NCPF cases with specific signs of portal hypertension; 58 biopsies in the preceding reproducibility step; 36 hypothetical scenarios for the diagnostic score
42191146.bottom_line: A multisociety consensus unifying PSVD and NCPF under one definition, making liver biopsy mandatory, setting adequacy at 15 mm with a 10 mm fragment, and defining nodular regenerative hyperplasia, muscularised portal venules and portal venule stenosis in 50% or more of portal tracts as major histological criteria - it establishes a shared vocabulary and reclassifies NRH as a marker of vascular disorder rather than a benign tumour, and it does not establish diagnostic validity for anything: the score was fitted to expert votes on 36 hypothetical scenarios and reproduced them by construction, the criteria were derived in 88 European patients who all had portal hypertension while the definition permits diagnosis without it, major criteria need only 10% sensitivity, and the term in the title carried 74% agreement against a pre-specified 75% threshold.

limitations: Significant statistical heterogeneity for the success outcome; although subgroup analyses were performed and the direction of effect was consistent, residual heterogeneity likely stems from variation in study protocols, definitions of treatment success, and technical details across trials
The inherent difficulty of blinding in trials of procedural interventions introduces potential performance bias, although the authors argue the objective nature of the primary outcomes mitigates this
Publication bias was not detected statistically but cannot be completely ruled out
critique: The methods state four databases were searched (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library in the abstract; PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection and Cochrane CENTRAL in the methods) and the results state 'our systematic search of the three electronic databases'. Embase is named in the abstract and absent from the methods list and the results - so the reader cannot determine whether the largest biomedical database was searched

The abstract states 'data were pooled using random-effects models' while the results state that for complications 'no significant heterogeneity was observed (I-squared = 46.1%, p=0.115)' and 'the pooled analysis using a fixed-effects model' was applied. The model used for the safety outcome contradicts the abstract, and an I-squared of 46% is treated as no heterogeneity on the basis of a 50% threshold the paper sets for itself

The safety conclusion - 'without increasing the risk of procedure-related complications' - rests on 7 of 12 trials and an odds ratio of 1.02 with a 95% interval of 0.30-3.50. That interval permits a 70% reduction or a 3.5-fold increase in complications. This is an uninformative result reported as equivalence, with no equivalence margin, no event counts given in the text and no power consideration

The pre-specified size subgroup that matters most is the one that fails. Eight of 12 trials studied 5-10 cm abscesses and the paper states the confidence interval for that subgroup crossed the line of no effect, while the >5 cm and >10 cm subgroups (3 trials between them) did not. The abstract instead says 'subgroup analyses by abscess size and etiology confirmed the consistency of this benefit' - which is true only of the direction of point estimates, not of statistical significance, and reverses the clinical reading for the majority of the data

The size subgroups are not mutually exclusive or coherently defined: '5-10', '>5' and '>10 cm' overlap, so a trial of 5-10 cm abscesses also satisfies >5 cm. Subgroup analysis across overlapping strata double-counts and cannot be interpreted as the paper does

Nine of 12 trials are Indian and 8 of 12 enrolled mixed amoebic-predominant abscesses treated with chloroquine or metronidazole. The pooled result is therefore principally about amoebic and mixed abscesses in India. Pyogenic abscess - the entity relevant to a Western incidental-liver-lesion pathway - is represented by 3 trials (Abusedera, Yu, Zerem) totalling 212 patients, and no pyogenic-only pooled estimate with its own interval is reported in the text

'Clinical treatment success' is never defined in the paper. The authors concede that varying definitions of treatment success across trials are a likely source of the 56% heterogeneity, which means the primary outcome of the meta-analysis has no single meaning. An OR of 4.12 on an undefined composite is not a transportable effect size

Trials span 1998-2023, a 25-year window across which imaging guidance, catheter technology (8F to 14F), antibiotic regimens and the threshold for intervention all changed. No meta-regression by year, catheter size or needle gauge is performed, although Table 1 records all of them

The largest trial contributes 543 of 1425 patients (38%) and is described in Table 1 as a 'Prospective randomized controlled trial' with 271 versus 272 patients and identical male counts in both arms (241/241) - an improbable exact balance that also appears in several other rows of Table 1 (Surya 44/44, Singh 26/27, Rajagopal 24/24, Kulhari 79/79, Rajak 19/19, Yu 19/19, Zerem 12/12). Perfect or near-perfect sex balance in eight of twelve trials is a pattern that warrants scrutiny of the primary data, and the review performs none

One included trial (Rajak 1998) enrolled patients aged 2-72 years and another (Singh 2009) aged 3-72, despite an inclusion criterion of age >=18. The eligibility rule was not applied to the included trials

Risk of bias is described only in prose and in two figures; no trial-level judgements are tabulated, no trial is identified as high risk, and no sensitivity analysis excluding trials at high risk or with unclear allocation concealment was performed, even though the authors state allocation concealment and blinding were frequently unclear

Needle aspiration protocols differ fundamentally between trials - some single aspiration, some repeated - and the review does not separate them, so part of the apparent PCD advantage may be an artefact of comparing continuous drainage with a single pass in some trials and with repeated passes in others
No GRADE assessment or certainty rating for either outcome, and no absolute risk difference or number needed to treat, despite an odds ratio of 4.12 being highly baseline-risk dependent
42743010.n: 12 RCTs, 1425 patients; 9 of the 12 trials conducted in India, publication years 1998-2023
42743010.bottom_line: Pooling 12 randomised trials and 1425 patients, mostly Indian and mostly with amoebic-predominant abscesses, percutaneous catheter drainage achieved roughly four times the odds of treatment success as needle aspiration (OR 4.12, 95% CI 2.01-8.45) with no detected difference in complications - it establishes catheter drainage as the preferred percutaneous technique for large or complex abscesses, and it does not establish safety equivalence (OR 1.02, CI 0.30-3.50, from 7 trials), nor a benefit in the 5-10 cm subgroup that comprises two thirds of the trials, nor any defined meaning for the 'treatment success' it pooled.
42743010.funding: No funding statement; the authors declare no conflicts of interest and state the datasets are available on request

limitations: Retrospective review of radiology reports rather than images; the authors state a more focused search of the images would have yielded additional cases, and scans were re-reviewed only when reports were unclear
Benignity was determined in most cases by stability at follow-up CT rather than histological confirmation, and a slow-growing metastasis would be misclassified as benign
10-mm collimation in 2793/2978 (93.8%) with no helical scanning available, so the actual number of small lesions was underestimated and the effective size threshold was raised
Monophasic contrast injection in most patients would also underestimate lesion number
Small lesions were certainly under-reported when larger metastases were also present, because attending radiologists do not describe each of multiple lesions individually

The distribution of primary tumours is atypical - lung cancer is under-represented because many such patients had only an extended thoracic CT covering part of the liver - so the series may not represent a typical metastatic population
Stage of disease was not controlled for, so the data cannot predict whether a given small lesion is more likely metastatic in the presence of extrahepatic metastases
Higher-prevalence figures in less common primaries must be interpreted cautiously because of small numbers
critique: The denominator is 2978 patients *who already have cancer and who had at least two abdominal CTs at a tertiary cancer centre*. Requiring a follow-up scan at the same institution conditions the cohort on surviving and remaining in follow-up, which preferentially removes patients with rapidly progressive disease - exactly the patients whose small lesions would have grown. This biases the 80.2% benign figure upward, and the paper does not address it

The 12.7% is a report-based prevalence, not a lesion prevalence. It measures how often a radiologist chose to write the phrase, which depends on reporting culture, not on how many sub-centimetre lesions existed. The authors concede a focused image search would find more

A pathway that quotes Schwartz's 12.7% next to Karhunen's 52%, Jones's 17% and Kaltenbach's 15% is comparing a report-mention rate in cancer patients on 10-mm CT, a targeted-autopsy rate in 95 Finnish men, a per-examination CT rate in cancer-surveillance outpatients, and a sonographic diagnosis rate in 45,319 hospital attenders. The four numbers are not interchangeable and happen to look similar only by coincidence

Benignity is defined circularly as 'did not grow on the same test', with no histology in any case. Since the 6-month stability threshold was chosen by the authors and 31 patients failed to meet it, the headline 11.6% metastatic rate is the most favourable of three analyses the authors themselves ran; the upper estimate of 19.8% - nearly one in five - is buried in the results

Table 1 reports the total as 3004 with 378 (12.4%) while the abstract reports 378/2978 (12.7%); the double-counting of 26 patients with two primaries is acknowledged for the total but not reconciled with the headline figure

The breast-cancer figure driving clinical anxiety (22% metastatic) rests on 14 events in 63 patients with small lesions; the melanoma row is 1 metastatic of 3 patients (33%) and the small-bowel row 1 of 2 (50%), and these per-tumour percentages are reported to the nearest whole number with no confidence intervals anywhere in the paper

The two subgroup comparisons that would most change management - extrahepatic metastases present vs absent, and solitary vs multiple - were both non-significant, yet the directional point estimates (36% vs 25.7%, 14.0% vs 9.8%) are the ones that get quoted. The study is underpowered for both and never reports a power calculation

The paper asserts 'there is no a priori reason to suspect that smaller, undetected lesions are more likely to be malignant' - an untested assumption that is load-bearing for transporting the result to thin-section helical CT, and that the authors call for studies on rather than demonstrate
Single institution, single scanner model (GE 9800), non-helical era; reader identity, number of readers and interobserver agreement are not reported
9885589.n: 2978 patients with cancer; 378 (12.7%) with small hepatic lesions reported
9885589.bottom_line: Among cancer patients at one tertiary centre with at least two CTs, a reported sub-centimetre hepatic lesion was metastatic in 11.6% (and up to 19.8% if indeterminates are counted as malignant) - it establishes that such lesions are usually but not reliably benign in known cancer, and establishes nothing about lesion prevalence, nothing about patients without cancer, and nothing verified by histology.
9885589.funding: Not stated; presented at the 1997 RSNA scientific assembly
